Katalog Berita (Halaman 54/57)

#780. Why unique Brighton defence is so tricky to unpick

Fabian Hurzeler got St Pauli promoted to the Bundesliga before leaving for Brighton in June 2024

"We have a great chance on Saturday to take revenge," were Fabian Hurzeler's words as Brighton exited the Carabao Cup at the hands of Manchester City.

The following Saturday, the 33-year-old's dogged defiance manifested in a 1-0 victory over the same opponents, who failed to score at home for the first time in 23 matches.

Brighton now sit in third place, only behind City and Premier League leaders Arsenal, both teams they have beaten this season.

And they have done so with a bravery and front-footedness that the likes of Arsenal and City have not always been used to facing.

Brighton's front-footedness has enabled them to win the ball back proactively, quickly turning moments of defence into attack

With 24 goals in nine games, Brighton are the league's top scorers but it is their defensive work that has underpinned their underdog victories against the league's best teams.

Notably, Brighton have conceded just seven goals this season - with only Arsenal conceding fewer.

From opposition goal-kicks, Brighton look to press high and in a man-to-man fashion. This is a common approach but Brighton's intensity across the pitch makes them better at executing this than most.

The challenge is that the opposition will have an extra player in their build-up compared to Brighton's 10 pressing outfielders, if they use their keeper as a passing option.

That potential issue is managed by one of Brighton's attackers leaving the centre-back they began marking - curving their run as they press the opposition keeper.

In curving their run, the aim is to cut off the passing angle back to they player they are no longer marking, while the rest of the team are responsible for their direct, individual opponents.

Charalampos Kostoulas first presses Gabriel Magalhaes before curving his run to press David Raya. This cuts off the pass back to Gabriel. The rest of the Brighton players are applying pressure in a man-to-man fashion.

Kostoulas' pressure on Raya forces him to kick the ball out of play early in the game

In spite of generally opting to play man-to-man across the pitch, at points in their build-up the team in possession may have an unmarked player.

This player is usually in an area of the pitch that is hard for them to access -Â such as their full-back or winger on the far side.

This is often an intentional decision Brighton take, believing the benefit of an extra pressing player closer to the ball is greater than the risk associated with leaving that opposing player unmarked.

By ensuring the opposing unmarked player is far from the ball, they reduce the likelihood that player is found. By putting more bodies around the ball, they increase the likelihood of winning the ball back.

Maxim de Cuyper curves his run as he presses Gianluigi Donnarumma. This makes it hard for City's keeper to pass it to Abdukodir Khusanov. With the angle to City's right side cut off, Brighton also leave Matheus Nunes, the far-side full-back, unmarked, knowing that finding him is difficult. Down City's left, they press man-to-man

What makes Brighton so unique though is how they defend deeper.

Most teams who press high from opposition goal-kicks then settle into a more rigid defensive shape closer to their own goal. These defensive blocks are generally examples of zonal defending rather than man-to-man defending.

The most common defensive block for top teams tends to come in the form of a 4-4-2. Players are tasked with marshalling specific 'zones', aiming to make it harder for opponents to get into dangerous positions. There is often a focus on blocking the centre of the pitch, with the wider areas less congested for opponents to play in.

Brighton's magic this season is in the form of continuing to use man-to-man ideas, albeit in a more measured fashion, when pushed closer to their own goal.

This more measured version of a man-to-man press is seen in Brighton's use of an extra player, or a 'plus-one' (+1) in their backline. Put simply, if opponents commit four forwards high up the pitch, Brighton will defend with five.

As such, Brighton aren't looking to go man-to-man everywhere, always, but they are looking to do it as much as they can while adhering to two key principles:Â trying to keep a plus-one in defence and while focusing on blocking the centre of the pitch.

In this example, we see almost every one of Brighton's defensive principles in one move. Here we see Brighton take a man-to-man approach from a deeper starting position

As Martin Odegaard dribbles deeper, Chema Andres, who began marking him, leaves the Arsenal captain to move back into midfield, providing central cover. As much as Brighton want to apply man-to-man pressure, they are also wary not to be pulled across the pitch in a way that leaves gaps in dangerous areas

In yellow, we see Brighton's man-to-man references in defence. In white, we see Brighton's spare player in defence. In blue, we see Chema, taking a more conservative, zonal defensive position, protecting the middle of the pitch

As Odegaard steps into a more dangerous position, Chema engages with him once again. Brighton are man-to-man across the pitch, while staying centrally compact. The only exception to their man-to-man defence here is the deliberately spare player at centre-back, Luka Vuskovic, highlighted in white

Odegaard passes the ball to Declan Rice, who is pressed by Yasin Ayari. Rice plays the ball into Kai Havertz, who is pressed by his respective marker stepping out of a centre-back position. Havertz is forced to play the ball back to Ezri Konsa

These ideas were seen clearly against Manchester City too.

In possession, Enzo Maresca asked right-back Matheus Nunes to push up and move infield, into a position that resembled a right-sided striker.

City, as well as the likes of Paris St-Germain and Arsenal, have used their full-backs in these unorthodox attacking positions as it poses difficult questions to the opponent who tracks them.

These players tend to find space as opposing wingers are typically less willing to track an attacking full-back all the way into their own box.

Hurzeler has used Maxim de Cuyper as his left winger this season, but the Belgian has played the majority of his career at left-back. This has equipped him with the work-rate and defensive nous to deal with the modern, roaming attacking full-back.

In man-to-man fashion, De Cuyper followed Nunes all the way into his fixed position higher up the pitch, and ended up defending at left centre-back - as Brighton created a back five. When Brighton had the ball, De Cuyper was back playing at left wing.

De Cuyper, Brighton's left winger, has tracked Nunes, City's right-back. This results in a Brighton back five. In white, we see Brighton's 'plus-one' player

Remember Brighton keeping a +1 at the back? Naturally, this leaves the other team with a spare player somewhere else. It is usually one of the opposition centre-backs who remain unmarked, finding themselves with time and space on the ball.

In an ideal situation, a centre-back less confident on the ball would be a good candidate to leave unmarked.

But even for impressive ball-playing defenders, the challenge is that every player they could pass to remains marked or could become marked in a fraction of a second based on how Brighton set-up.

Brighton are also continually shifting, looking to find moments in which one player can spring to press the unmarked centre-back on the ball. When this jump happens, Brighton will lock on to a full man-to-man press, looking to force a turnover or push the opposition back towards their keeper.

Ayari turns to notice Bruno Guimaraes' position

De Cuyper turns to notice Jurrien Timber, free at right-back. These looks help the Brighton players organise their man-oriented press

De Cuyper's attention is drawn to Timber. Pascal Gross presses Rice and Ayari is blocking the pass into Guimaraes. The pass back to Konsa triggers Ayari to step up on to Rice as Gross applies pressure to the previously unmarked Konsa

This ends up looking like a vertical domino effect across the pitch. Chema then steps up from a holding midfield position to press Guimaraes. Brighton have ended up man-to-man around the ball

There are solutions to this organised yet man-oriented defending and Abdukodir Khusanov's powerful ball-carrying from a wider position was perhaps the best Manchester City had on show.

But combining key principles in the form of blocking the centre of the pitch and not being baited into mindlessly tracking players looking to stretch their shape, while still locking on to individual players nearby, make Brighton an incredibly difficult puzzle for teams to solve.

For as potent as they have been in attack, it is their bravery in defence that has given them the platform.

#779. Another 1-0 for relentless Arsenal - but did Odegaard spare VAR blushes?

Odegaard's strike enough for Arsenal to get past Hull

It was not pretty, but Martin Odegaard's goal was enough to secure the 1-0 win that ensured Arsenal go into the international break as the Premier League leaders.

It was Arsenal's 34th 1-0 win under Mikel Arteta, to equal their best start to a Premier League season under the Spaniard of 27 points earned after 10 games in 2022-23.

No team has enjoyed more 1-0 wins since Arteta was appointed back in 2019, with the Gunners winning their past 10 home games in all competitions, keeping eight clean sheets in that time.

Odegaard's goal though, bundled home from close range, may well have been a relief to those at Pro Ref, too.

A controversial video assistant referee (VAR) decision, which denied the Gunners a first-half penalty, threatened to be the story as a largely uneventful game drifted by.

When referee Farai Hallam was sent to the pitchside monitor for a VAR review for a shirt pull by Nobel Mendy on Kai Havertz, surely everyone inside the Emirates was expecting a penalty.

The irony would not be lost on Liverpool fans, who were denied a VAR penalty for a shirt pull last weekend when Arsenal's Jurrien Timber tugged back Alexander Isak.

Unlike Isak, Havertz made sure everyone - including VAR Michael Oliver, was aware that a defender had hold of his shirt.

Indeed, the cheers had already begun when Hallam started to describe the foul to the crowd - but Gunners supporters were stopped in their tracks. The referee pivoted to an offside against Havertz, and play restarted with a free-kick to Hull.

Had Arsenal not mustered that 72nd-minute winner from their captain, much of the attention would, once again, have been on VAR.

Tottenham set to complain to Pro Ref - but should Bogle have seen red?

Odegaard hits winner as Arsenal beat Hull to extend lead at top

Mikel Arteta post-match interview - Arsenal v Hull

If Arsenal had dropped points, it wouldn't have been the first time this weekend that a match would have been dominated by discussions about the video officials.

On Friday, Coventry City were denied what appeared to be a clear penalty against Everton for a hair pull by James Tarkowski on Caleb Yirenkyi. Then in the second half, when Thierno Barry scored to put the Toffees 2-1 up and the ball appeared to come off his hand.

The controversy continued in Saturday's early kick-off between Leeds and Tottenham. First, Leeds wanted a penalty for handball by Mateus Fernandes, though replays did show the ball hit the Spurs player's shoulder.

Then came the potential red card for a challenge by Jayden Bogle on Mathys Tel, which has split opinion. The VAR, Tony Harrington, eventually decided after a four-minute VAR check that the foul did not have enough force.

That Tel was forced off injured, and referee John Brooks did not even show a yellow card on the field, only added to the frustration for Tottenham.

So on to the Emirates, and again the debate was around VAR.

It's a situation few would question. After all, an offside player winning a penalty surely goes against the very logic of the law?

If an offside player is running to the ball and is fouled before they attempt to play the ball or challenge an opponent, then the foul is considered to come before the offside offence.

The law seeks to prevent situations whereby defenders have carte blanche to foul attackers, just because the opponent is offside.

Former Premier League assistant referee Darren Cann told BBC Match of the Day: âThe foul should have taken precedence over the offside and it should have been a penalty. The law is very ambiguous though.â

But is a complex area of law and is very much open to interpretation.

In February 2019, the season before VAR came in, an offside Harry Kane was awarded a late penalty in a north London derby after being dragged down by Shkodran Mustafi.

Two years ago, Newcastle were awarded a spot-kick against Bournemouth through a VAR intervention when Adam Smith tugged back an offside Fabian Schar.

Yet last December, after being awarded a penalty against Leeds, Brentford's Dango Ouattara was ruled to be offside and the spot-kick ruled out through VAR.

So which interpretation is correct? Kane and Schar, or Havertz and Ouattara?

Ouattara was somewhat different, as he appeared to be engaging with Gabriel Gudmundsson as the ball was played.

The Havertz example is more like the one involving Schar, who was running forward when his shirt was tugged back.

But there is an additional consideration, and this is where Oliver's thinking will lie.

Officials are asked to consider the likelihood of the attacker becoming involved in the play from a second phase. Let's say the ball could be first played by a team-mate, which then makes them onside. Then they are not purely benefitting from being offside.

In the case of Schar and Kane, they could have benefitted from that second phase.

Havertz was the only attacker who had any chance of being involved in the play, so the VAR determined offside was the fair outcome.

At least tonight most of the talk will be about another victory for Arsenal - and not VAR.

Goal caps eye-catching Odegaard display - player ratings for Arsenal v Hull

Another game, another win but still Arsenal are looking for their attack to spark into life.

At the end of the day results matter but Arsenal, despite being top, are the lowest scorers of the teams in the top four.

They have the best defence in the league and arguably Europe but goals are also seeming hard to come by at the other end.

Arsenal have not scored more than twice in the league since the opening day of the season, when they put three past Coventry.

Arteta's side are missing talisman Bukayo Saka, who is out with a quadricep injury, and has a unique partnership with Ben White and Martin Odegaard on the right.

On the left Christos Tzolis started the season well but, after a hamstring injury while playing for Greece, the 24-year-old has not looked the same threat.

The same can be said for Kai Havertz too.

The 27-year-old picked up a hamstring injury playing for Germany and, even though he scored the winner against Liverpool, his performances have not reached the same level.

Viktor Gyokeres is firmly second choice this season and Arteta is still working out how to get the best out of the maverick Eberechi Eze, while Noni Madueke is working to fill the gap left by Saka.

Arteta was asked about the number of single-goal wins this season and what he can do to improve that.

"To be more efficient," was the answer the Gunners boss gave. "We are one against one against the keeper. That's happened twice today.

"There is a penalty there, there is another situation inside the box where the ball is bouncing. So many shots that have been deflected, blocked. We need to find ways to be more efficient, sometimes even more pragmatic.

"Sometimes my feeling is that we are trying to score a perfect goal against these low blocks. We need to be much more chaotic than that, and that's it. And open, I think, score much earlier because obviously that's going to change the course of the game."

Even if the Gunners could be more free-flowing going forward, they have started the season in a formidable way - winning nine of their 10 league games.

And if they manage to keep up that rate of winning, the Gunners will likely defend their Premier League crown and win back-to-back titles for the first time in 100 years.

#778. Is Kylie Kelce Ready for Baby No. 5 With Jason Kelce?

Kylie Kelce—mom to daughters Wyatt, 7, Elliotte, 5, Bennett, 3, and Finnley, 19 months, with husband Jason Kelce—addressed whether she's considering expanding their family once more: "We enjoy chaos."

Kylie Kelce is not gonna lie about her thoughts on adding another player to her team.

The 34-year-old—who shares daughters Wyatt, 7, Elliotte, 5, Bennett, 3, and Finnley, 19 months, with husband Jason Kelce—weighed in on the possibility of having a fifth baby in the future.

“It’s funny,” Kylie shared on the Nov. 4 episode of her Not Gonna Lie podcast when her guest Joanna Gaines asked if she’d be open to having more kids. “That was one of the questions that we talked about.”

As a mom of five herself, Joanna—who shares kids Drake, 21, Ella, 20, Duke, 18, Emmie, 16, and Crew, 8, with husband Chip Gaines—encouraged Kylie to have one more kid.

“Five is a good number,” the Fixer Upper star noted to Kylie, who asked, “Is it?”

“And it’s gonna be a boy,” Joanna added. “I think you should do it.”

While Kylie laughed at the interior designer’s quip about the possibility of having a boy after four girls, she appeared intrigued, especially when Joanna noted that she thinks Kylie and Jason—who married in 2018—“thrive in chaos.”

“We do,” Kylie admitted. “We enjoy chaos.”

“You think one more?” the podcast host asked Joanna with a smile, to which the HGTV star  replied, “Yes, obviously, give it some time.”

“Kylie, bust it out, five,” she continued, adding further encouragement. “It’s gonna be your little boy and it's gonna rock your world because it's totally different than girls and it's another spot in your heart. Or if it's a girl, great, ‘cause five girls is a party house.”

And Kylie couldn’t help but highlight that the number five does have quite the ring to it, especially in sports terms.

After all, she noted, “It's a starting five, isn't it?”

Although the Not Gonna Lie host didn’t give a direct answer about expanding her and Jason’s team, she did make it clear that she was taking Joanna’s words to heart.

“OK, if we have a fifth child, I'm gonna come right back to this moment right here,” Kylie shared with a laugh, before joking, “‘Jo did it!’”

But Joanna ended the topic by throwing in one last play.

As she told Kylie, “Let me do the nursery!”

While time will tell what the future holds, Kylie didn’t hesitate to tackle the bodyshamers who speculated she was expecting over the summer after she shared photos from a trip to Paris.

“Stop trying to get me to have more. Stop it,” she stressed on a July 30 episode of Not Gonna Lie. “That's between me, my husband, and my motherf--king uterus.”

As she emphasized, “Even if, which I am not, even if I was with child, that is between me and my husband to decide when we would like to share that information.”

For a closer look at Kylie and Jason’s huddle of six, keep reading…

In October 2019, Jason Kelce and Kylie Kelce welcomed their first baby together, a daughter named Wyatt Elizabeth Kelce.

Their second daughter Elliotte Ray Kelce joined the family two years later.

One year after Elliotte's arrival, Kylie shared that "another Kelce lady" would be added to the bunch with an adorable set of photos.

On Halloween 2022, Jason and a then-pregnant Kylie dressed up as Piglet and Kanga, respectively. Meanwhile, their girls were Tigger and Winne the Pooh.

In February 2023, the couple welcomed their third child, with her arrival coming nearly two weeks after Jason faced off against brother Travis Kelce at the 2023 Super Bowl.

Jason shared a glimpse at his oldest daughters holding a huge prize in May 2023, writing on Instagram, "Never in a million years did I think I’d hold the Larry O’Brien trophy, let alone that it would be in my house!!"

"Unbelievable honor to see it in person," he continued. "The size is incredible, looks so small when NBA players are holding it, but it’s actually massive!! The girls were very interested in it."

The family of five hit the field in August 2023, with Kylie joking in an Instagram post, "Here for the Rita’s and obstacle courses with dad after practice."

Jason and Kylie rang in Wyatt's fourth birthday in October 2023 on the Philadelphia Eagles' home turf. As Kylie noted on Instagram, "We were celebrating a 4th birthday when the Birds went 4-0."

Kylie shared this pic of Wyatt, Elliotte and Bennett on Instagram in June 2024, writing, "Parents know… 2 out of 3 isn’t bad!"

Jason's mom Donna Kelce commented, "The cutest beautiful bunch of 'lucky charms' under that rainbow!!!!"

Jason and Kylie welcomed their fourth baby girl Finnley "Finn" Anne Kelce on March 30, 2025.

Kylie craddled her Finn in her arms after the baby's March 2025 arrival.

Little Finn rocked a floral onesie shortly after she was born in the hospital.

The Philadelphia Eagles alum held newborn Finnley close in an Instagram photo shared in April 2025.

#777. Enzo Maresca rues Manchester City’s lack of desire after defeat at Nottingham Forest

‘You need desire and intensity … we didn’t match them’

City have now lost three successive league matches

Enzo Maresca blamed his side’s lack of desire and the way they were outgunned in duels for a third successive Premier League defeat. After winning their first seven games of the season, Manchester City’s 3-1 loss at Nottingham Forest extended their poor run.

Jair Cunha dispossessed Josko Gvardiol to score the opener, then Liam Delap struck twice with muscular surges on the break as Forest won their first home league game since April. “Today I think [the problem] has been general,” said Maresca. “It’s not about one player. In the first half we lost all the duels, all the contacts. Against this team, that is fighting relegation, if you don’t match them … it’s something we need to understand. In this kind of game, if you’re not able to win duels and second balls like in the first half, you struggle.

“You need desire and intensity to win second balls and duels. You require intensity or you struggle and we didn’t match their intensity. The second and third goals are copy and paste, lost duels first in the middle of pitch then at the edge of the box.”

City’s 100% record came to an end with a 2-1 defeat away by Aston Villa, and they followed that up last week with a 1-0 home reverse against Brighton. “They are all different,” said Maresca. “But if you look at chances, possession, chances inside box, in all of them we were much, much better but we lost all of them. We’re going to use this international break to clarify what we can do better. We know we need to improve things and avoid this kind of game.”

After his frustrated reaction to last week’s defeat at Brentford, Oliver Glasner was understandably delighted that his reset, ending what he had referred to as compromises, had paid off.

“The way we play football I think we’ve had many better games,” he said. “But how we defended, how passionately we defended, how tactically smart we defended, it was one of our better games.

“You should control everything and if you want to control it, you have to run because you have to be so quickly aware – they’re so good, such great players, such a good structure and they move the ball so quickly. Of course, you can just defend but you also need to go forward and this is what we did today in the right moments.”

#776. Last season difficult with injury and miscarriage - Muniz

Fulham save a point late on against struggling Newcastle

Fulham striker Rodrigo Muniz has spoken of the struggles he endured last season, revealing his wife suffered a miscarriage.

Muniz scored the equaliser for the Cottagers in a 1-1 draw against Newcastle United on Saturday for his first league goal since their opening top-flight match of last season.

"Last season was really difficult for me because, now I can say it, but I had the surgery," said the 25-year-old Brazilian, who had an operation on a hamstring injury, external in November and was out until early February.

"My wife was pregnant last season and, unfortunately, we lost the baby, but God is good all the time and now she's pregnant again.

"The goal was for my baby, and I hope this season will be different than last season."

Muniz also scored in wins over AFC Wimbledon and West Ham in the Carabao Cup this season.

Overall, he has 19 goals and three assists in 86 Premier League appearances for the London club since joining from Flamengo in 2021.

"I train hard every week to get opportunities to play and I want to play more," said Muniz, whose eight Premier League appearances under manager Alvaro Arbeloa this season have all come off the bench.

"I cannot control the gaffer, but I showed the gaffer I want to play more. I have to keep training hard, for him to say, 'OK, now is your time', and then I'm ready."

#775. Julián Alvarez’s Atlético redemption arc in full focus for visit of Barcelona

Top spot is up for grabs in Sunday’s heavyweight clash as the Spider faces the team that tried to trap him last summer

Julián Alvarez said sorry but forgiveness must be earned on the field and Sunday would be the perfect place. At 9pm at the Metropolitano, Atlético Madrid play Barcelona. It is the biggest match in Spain right now, a place at the top of the table awaiting the winner; it is also the game the striker they call the Spider planned to play on the other side. That, Alvarez said in Dallas, was his “dream”. Denied that, he must defeat the men he wanted to join to win back the supporters he wanted to walk out on, no better opportunity than now.

He has beaten them before. Last season, Atlético knocked Barcelona out of the Copa del Rey and Champions League. Alvarez scored both times but beneath the surface something had shifted in him and by the time the World Cup came round he admitted his desire to leave for Catalonia. That day, after Argentina beat Algeria, he didn’t name Barcelona and he didn’t need to; everyone knew. “It’s not the time to talk about this but nor can I hide,” he said. “I spoke with the people I needed to and the best thing for everyone is a transfer.”

Turned out that wasn’t true. Atlético didn’t agree then, refusing to sell; Barcelona, so open in their pursuit at the time, may not agree now. In week two of the new season, Alvarez was still in Madrid, whistled and booed by his own supporters, invited to walk off up the tunnel alone while his teammates turned the other way to applaud the fans who had abused him. One chant had started: “Tell him to go,” to which Alvarez probably thought: I’m trying. He had cut a lonely, distant figure, and if that was partly a public staging of his discontent, one more attempt to force his way out, if the fact he didn’t turn up for training over the next two days was as well, it didn’t work: when the transfer window shut six days later, he was still there.

They were still whistling too. Stuck, Alvarez had some making up to do, if only out of convenience, if only for a little while. He left Fernando Hidalgo, the agent whose exit strategy had failed, whom Atlético’s chief executive accused of having led Alvarez astray and who responded by calling the club “liars”. That helped, handing over someone to blame. He also played a bit more and a bit better, if not much to begin with. He at last scored a goal against Stuttgart on 20 October and four days later did it again, this time at home in a 1-0 win over Deportivo A Coruña. “I would like to apologise to our people for my words at the World Cup,” he said after.

Alvarez didn’t deny the way he felt and didn’t say that he no longer wanted to depart, but he did say he had made a mistake in the how and when. “I understand the anger; as a fan I would have been angry too, especially after all they had done to support me,” he said. The coach, Diego Simeone, was relieved. “I am very respectful of those who say sorry because it is not easy to say sorry,” he said. “I am sure Julián is more at peace now.”

It was about time, most fans felt, the least Alvarez could do – four months had passed since that day in Dallas, six weeks since he definitively realised he was staying – but he had waited until there was a goal, a peace offering to go with it. They had cheered it of course, but that didn’t mean embracing him. They also knew, though, that he was probably their best player. “We need lots of goals from Julián to be up there,” Jan Oblak had said in Stuttgart. “He has the quality to score a thousand goals,” Álex Grimaldo said.

He hasn’t yet but it is getting better, if slowly. Having started one of the first seven games, and without getting a goal, he has started five out of eight since, scoring twice. Meanwhile Barcelona, who thought they needed his goals, haven’t.

The summer in which they lost Robert Lewandowski, Marcus Rashford and Ferran Torres, and lost out on Alvarez, led to the reinvention of Raphinha as a No 9 and he is Europe’s top scorer with 19. Nor is it just him: people asked who was going to get the goals; the answer was everyone. Lamine Yamal has 13 goals and 11 assists. Thirteen different players have scored. Barcelona are on course to get more than 150 in the league alone, the chances of them returning for Alvarez receding. Barcelona are all right without him. The clásico reverse was their only domestic defeat after nine straight wins, although that same week they lost in Paris too, and the way it happened revealed a vulnerability.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Hope too for Atlético, for whom things were falling into place. Simeone had to accept Bayern Munich were superior on Tuesday, a step above that they cannot take yet, but in La Liga they have won seven in a row, including victory over their city rivals, Real. There is an assuredness about them, a variety too, optimism. Their record is better than it was at this stage the last time they won the league, the same question bringing the same answer. Who is going to get the goals? Everyone. Alvarez has scored one in the league, but Álex Baena has five, Álex Grimaldo four, Jonathan David and Giuliano Simeone three.

And here they are, ahead of Madrid, and just behind Barcelona. They have done it without the best Alvarez, the Spider’s powers weakened but slowly returning as he accepts that this is his place, begins a mission to make amends. Diminishing dependency may be no bad thing, the striker recast instead as an addition, the final, recovered piece in a functioning team, imagination allowed to take flight. Imagine if they can get him back; imagine if he can win them back too. Imagine if it happened on Sunday, with the win that takes Atlético to the top, redemption and rise in one, reconciliation too. “If the club wants to be in the places the fans dream of, we’ll need Julián,” Simeone said, no time like now.

#774. Is there something missing despite Rangers' impressive form?

Rangers have won 10 and drawn two of their past 12 matches in all competitions

Rangers are unbeaten in their past 12 matches in all competitions, winning 10 of them, and moved to within a point of the Scottish Premiership summit after Saturday's 2-0 win away to St Mirren.

They thoroughly deserved their victory. They have the best defensive record in the top flight and the third best attacking record, but it feels as though they are not playing to their full potential.

In Paisley, Derek McInnes' side never quite put the game to bed despite a host of chances and St Mirren should really have pulled one back in the closing stages.

"There's still not that element of control," former Celtic striker Chris Sutton said on Sky Sports.

"That killer instinct is really important, but they don't control games the way they should. That will be the worry. Eventually that will bite Rangers in the backside."

Sutton's sparring partner on Sky - former Rangers and Scotland striker Kris Boyd - agreed.

"They are a good team, but with Rangers teams of the past, that would have been three or four," he said.

Rangers overcome St Mirren to move point behind Celtic

Ryan Naderi - who put Rangers in front from the penalty spot and has scored six in his past eight league matches - should have scored before he did.

Strike partner Kevin Kelsy missed a host of chances at the start of the second half before midfielder Dan Neil's deflected shot nestled in the bottom corner to make it 2-0.

Rangers' expected goals in their 12 league matches this season is 29.8. They have scored just 21.

Key striking duo Youssef Chermiti and Lawrence Shankland are both out injured and that goes some way to explaining their profligacy in front of goal, but it doesn't tell the full story.

Naderi and Kelsy have performed admirably this season - there have only been two matches since August in which neither man has scored.

It is the players behind them who have not fully stepped up to the plate.

South Korean winger Kim Min-su is yet to score or assist in Rangers colours since signing from Girona in the summer, although he created more chances than any other player on Saturday, while Badredine Bouanani has shown undoubted quality without regularly delivering end product.

Against St Mirren, there were plenty of promising attacking positions that did not result in a shot as players took the wrong option and allowed the home defence to recover.

As McInnes pointed out: "Loads of chances. It's quite ironic we scored from a penalty and a deflected shot, but some of our work was really clean up until the last part.

"What becomes a good chance could be a brilliant chance if we just take care with the weight of pass and make the right decision.

"There are umpteen examples in that game today and it's something we need to improve on. We've got to take ownership that we can do better in these moments.

"The top players make these decisions at breakneck speed and pick the right pass."

It is obviously something McInnes has impressed on his players and Neil referenced the need to be more ruthless.

"We speak all the time about being more clinical and there were a couple of chances we could have done better with," the former Sunderland midfielder said.

McInnes - who fell agonisingly short of winning the title with Heart of Midlothian last season - was open about how he wants and expects more from his players moving forwards, despite their impressive form.

"It's not been perfect," he said of the past two and a half months. "We've had the draw with Hearts and the draw at Dundee.

"Our fight is with ourselves to keep improving. If we can keep winning and getting those improvements as we go along, there's hopefully more to come from us."

If those improvements do come, Sutton believes Rangers could be hard to stop.

"They seem like a team that have another gear or two and that will be a worry for the other teams in the league," he added.

#773. Liverpool v Arsenal: Women’s Super League – live

⚽️ Women’s Super League updates from 12pm GMT ⚽️ Océane Hurtré making waves at Birmingham | Email Emillia

And, breathe… That was a brilliant half of football. Although Arsenal lead, it still feels like this could go either way.

Arsenal lead at the break following an action-packed first half.

45+1 min: That goal came at a great time for Arsenal. They will lead going into the break.

Russo strikes again for Arsenal! Baum sends a cross into the box and the striker gets to it first, directing a header into the bottom-left corner.

44 min: The Gunners make their way forward and pass the ball around the Liverpool box, but struggle to cause a threat before the Reds break it down.

41 min: Arsenal appear to have a bit more momentum as we head into the final minutes of this half. But, if we’ve learned anything from this season, it’s that any team can strike against them at any moment.

38 min: Arsenal break forward as Hinds plays a pass through to Foord on the left. The winger makes her way to the byline before cutting the ball back to Smith, whose shot is excellently blocked by Fisk.

35 min: That disallowed Liverpool goal is a tough one to call. It’s very difficult to see – even with replays – if the ball came off Endemann or Catley.

If it was Catley, that goal should have stood and it’s very unlucky for the hosts.

32 min: Arsenal seem to have regained their fire – I’m not sure what took them so long. The intensity has increased again and they are now starting to put more pressure on the Liverpool defence.

29 min: Arsenal head straight down to the other end of the pitch as Russo plays Foord through, but the winger’s effort is sent wide.

28 min: Liverpool have the ball in the net – but it won’t count! After Arsenal fail to clear a corner away, Jenna Clark pounces to fire the ball into the net, but Endemann is deemed to be in an offside position.

27 min: Liverpool have a free kick in a dangerous position following a foul just outside the box.

Ramos takes it and forces a good save from Rodríguez.

26 min: Endemann sends a cross into the box from the right, but Williamson manages to scoop it away.

24 min: It took a while for Liverpool to grow into the game but they are playing very well now. Arsenal, meanwhile, have massively dropped off.

21 min: Liverpool are on the front foot now. They have had the most possession since that opening goal and are having more touches in the opposition box.

If any team looks likely to get a second, it’s the hosts.

18 min: As soon as Arsenal scored that opener, they took their foot off the gas. The intensity dropped and that has allowed Liverpool to gain momentum.

They could’ve built on that lead with the way they were playing but instead they have let it slip and now they are under pressure.

16 min: Ramos plays a long ball straight through the heart of the Arsenal midfield and defence to Olsson, who eases her way past Williamson before slotting her shot into the bottom-left corner.

I can’t help but think Williamson could’ve done better there. She appeared to let Olsson run straight through.

That was some poor defending from Arsenal.

14 min: An interesting replay has just been shown from that Arsenal goal. As the cross was sent in, Smith appeared to pull the shirt of a Liverpool player, stopping them from intercepting the ball. That allowed Russo to get the shot away.

If we had VAR in the league, that could have been disallowed.

12 min: Arsenal have settled a bit more following that goal. Liverpool are being given a bit more space to play.

9 min: Fox makes a good run to the byline before playing a low cross into the box, where she finds Russo on the penalty spot. The striker – who has started the game in the No10 position – then drills her shot into the bottom-left corner with her first touch.

Alessia Russo breaks the deadlock for Arsenal!

The Gunners have been piling on the pressure so far and it has paid off.

6 min: This match has not been short of action so far! Smith is next to run through on goal but blasts her effort wide and over the crossbar from a tight angle.

5 min: Huge chance for the visitors as Baum goes for goal inside the box, but her effort takes a huge deflection off the shoulder of Kerr and rattles the crossbar!

4 min: Arsenal head straight back down to the other end of the pitch as Baum shrugs off Bernabé before winning a corner.

3 min: Endemann looks to send a cross towards the back post from the right but the ball runs behind.

2 min: Arsenal drive forward early and look to pile on the pressure. They move the ball around the edge of the Liverpool box before Baum makes a run to the byline, but the ball runs behind for a goal kick.

That period of silence was impeccably observed. Now, on to kick-off.

The teams are out and kick-off is just a few moments away. But first, everybody will observe a period of silence for Remembrance Sunday.

It will be interesting to see today if Alessia Russo starts as the lone striker, or in the No10 position.

Renée Slegers has been persevering with Russo in the 10 for much of the season so far. I do wonder if that could be a reason for Arsenal’s lack of goals. There is absolutely no doubt that the 27-year-old is at her best when she’s playing as a No9.

Manchester City returned to the top of the WSL table yesterday with a 5-0 win over West Ham, while Chelsea dropped points against Everton.

Liverpool starting line-up: Khiara Keating; Sam Kerr, Grace Fisk (C), Jenna Clark, Alejandra Bernabé; Fūka Nagano, Natalia Ramos, Kirsty Maclean; Vivien Endemann, Cornelia Kapocs, Beata Olsson.

Subs: Faye Kirby, Lucy Parry, Marie Höbinger, Sara Agrež, Alice Bergström, Mao Itamura, Mari Ward, Zara Shaw, Maizie Trueman.

Arsenal starting line-up: Misa Rodríguez, Emily Fox, Leah Williamson, Steph Catley, Taylor Hinds; Kim Little (C), Georgia Stanway, Lisa Baum; Olivia Smith, Caitlin Foord, Alessia Russo.

Subs: Daphne van Domselaar, Anneke Borbe, Lotte Wubben-Moy, Élisa De Almeida, Smilla Holmberg, Kyra Cooney-Cross, Géraldine Reuteler, Frida Maanum, Mia Dixon.

Hello and welcome to coverage of Liverpool v Arsenal in the Women’s Super League. Both teams are in desperate need of a win as they look to climb up the WSL table, with the Reds in 11th and the Gunners in eighth.

Liverpool come into this game having not managed a league win since September 27 – and last weekend’s heavy 4-1 loss to West Ham will be on their minds.

Meanwhile, following a poor start to the season, the Gunners enjoyed two successive wins against Tottenham and Benfica but saw their form drop once more in a 1-1 draw against Aston Villa. Renée Slegers now finds herself under increasing pressure, meaning a win today is vital.

#771. Can we regrow damaged seagrass meadows?

Seagrass protects coasts, shelters thousands of species and stores CO2. But some 30% of this valuable ecosystem has disappeared since the late 19th century. Can we bring it back?

Half a dozen divers are navigating the cold waters of the Baltic Sea off the coast of Dahme, a small beach town in northern Germany. Keeping the roots intact, conservationists carefully lift shoots from a donor meadow of seagrass and place them in a bag.

They only take a few shoots from each spot, which will be planted where the conservationists hope to regrow another meadow. They've already picked out a prime area for the young plants, which need sandy sediment, shelter from waves and currents and sufficient light and oxygen to thrive.

The scientists see the work as critical. Myriam Spicka, who heads the NGO Seagrass Conservation, says she has "seen the changes" in the more than 30 years she's been diving. And she is not the only one who has witnessed the destruction.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Scientists estimate that around 60% of the Baltic coast's seagrass meadows have disappeared.

"That's the bad news," said marine ecologist Thorsten Reusch from the GEOMAR Helmholtz Center for Ocean Research Kiel . "The good news is that the decline has stopped."

Underwater seagrass meadows feed and shelter fish, crabs, shellfish and many other species. They improve water quality and slow waves, helping protect shores from erosion. And they store carbon in the seabed about 30 to 50 times faster than forests.

Around 70 species of seagrass can be found along the coasts of more than 150 countries. Some grow just below the surface, others at depths of 60 meters or almost 200 feet.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Some countries have far more seagrass, particularly in the Indo-Pacific," said Reusch. "There, it can play a major role in their carbon balance."

But the value of seagrass goes beyond carbon storage. Its meadows in the Baltic are among the sea's most valuable habitats. They shelter wildlife, stabilize the seabed and act as natural filters by trapping particles and nutrients.

Planting individual seagrass shoots is painstaking work so people like Reinhard Helbig are trying to make it easier.

Through ZosteraTec, the start-up he co-founded, he helps restore marine habitats, including seagrass meadows damaged by offshore activity, such as wind farm construction. His work begins on the beach.

"Stormy weather helps us. Waves and currents wash seagrass out of the seabed. A day or two later, it washes up here, still fresh," he said.

The collected shoots are grown and multiplied in ZosteraTec's aquaculture. Several months later, the marine saplings are laid on a plant support. A specially developed machine binds the planted strands with biodegradable thread. The resulting lengths can be laid on the seabed with less diving work.

"We plant here on land to cut down on underwater work. That means fewer dives, and we can do the painstaking work on shore," Helbig said.

Researchers at the Geomar Helmholtz Center in Kiel are also testing new ways to restore seagrass across larger areas, including using seeds.

Marine ecologist Esther Thomsen reaches into an aquarium tank and pulls out a flowerpot containing seagrass.

"Ten percent of the plants in our meadows produce seeds. You can clearly see the seeds sitting inside the seed pod," she said.

"The big advantage of restoring meadows from seed is greater genetic diversity. And in the future, we should be able to sow seeds over much larger areas," explained Thomsen.

Reusch from Geomar said they currently "think the most promising way to grow meadows that can withstand climate change is to plant individual shoots as a foundation, then sow seeds between them to increase genetic diversity."

Whether a planting mission is successful is revealed months or even years later.

Thomsen and her colleagues are visiting the first seagrass meadow planted in Germany's Baltic waters in 2021. The divers count shoots, check how densely they grow and record how the meadow has developed.

They then compare it with the donor meadow that supplied the plants. Only that comparison reveals whether the new crop has merely survived or is beginning to function more like a natural one.

"We've just checked the seagrass meadow, and it's really dense. We counted lots of shoots per square," Thomsen said. "It's looking really good."

This article is based on a Global Us video report.

#770. Maresca's dream start turns into nightmare as title hopes hit

Delap brace inspires Forest to stunning win over Man City

Enzo Maresca left the City Ground on Saturday evening with chants of "can we play you every week?" ringing in his ears - and the Italian's dream start as Manchester City manager is rapidly turning into a nightmare.

Amid a sea of noise from the home faithful on the banks of the River Trent, the delirious Forest supporters witnessed their side produce a thrilling performance as City sunk to a third straight Premier League loss.

Maresca's leaky backline continues to make defensive blunders and once Josko Gvardiol gave the ball away for Jair Cunha to open the scoring in the sixth minute, City were on the back foot.

With Arsenal edging past Hull earlier in the day and keeping another clean sheet, City head into the international break searching for answers after a 3-1 loss and six points behind the champions.

Maresca said: "The first half we didn't match [Forest's] intensity or win duels or second balls. The first thing required in these games is intensity.

"We tried to react at 2-0 but it's too late. We scored one, probably could have scored more but in transition we concede one more. No panic. We need to understand but no panic."

Asked why the intensity was low, Maresca replied: "I need to analyse that."

The situation already looks bleak for City, but what does history show?

Should Brighton fail to beat Brentford on Sunday, Arsenal would be just the fourth side in Premier League history to have a six-point lead after 10 games, while only two teams have been so far behind as City at this stage and gone on to win the title.

One of those was Manchester United in 2002-03. The other? City themselves in 2013-14 under Manuel Pellegrini.

But Fabian Hurzeler's Brighton have the opportunity to leap up to second place and five points behind the Gunners should they beat Brentford.

There is another factor which looms large over City's campaign.

The club have lodged an appeal after being found guilty of breaking Premier League financial rules.

That process is ongoing - and it is not yet known what potential sanctions City could face.

But - even if any possible punishment does not affect this season - their title hopes are looking slimmer by the match.

Delightful Delap and outfought Anderson - Forest v Man City player ratings

Has Anderson lived up to the hype after Man City move?

With his hands tucked inside his trouser pockets and his head bowed, a forlorn-looking Maresca paced the touchline towards the end of the match.

The City boss said during the week he was still getting to know his players, but performances like the one against Forest will provide some clarity as to who he can, and cannot, trust.

After starting the season with seven straight wins, City have hit real trouble with defeats against Aston Villa, Brighton and now a pumped-up Forest.

Their problems at the back are not helping as it was another game where individual errors cost them dearly - and former striker Liam Delap took full advantage of the lapses in concentration with two goals.

Gvardiol was at fault for the first, Iliman Ndiaye and Elliot Anderson got in a muddle for the second, while Matheus Nunes did not put a challenge in for the third.

"Before the game all the talk was about individual errors," former Forest winger Steve Stone told BBC Radio 5 Live. "Apart from the first goal, this hasn't been about that - the line is disjointed.

"The full-backs were very wide. If the ball turns over quickly and you pass it with your first pass you can be right through them. They have been exposed today.

"Oliver Glasner's team have played through them every time."

It was a miserable return to the City Ground for Anderson since his Â£116m move to City in the summer and the midfield dynamic alongside Enzo Fernandez does not seem to be working.

The Argentine should have scored with a headed chance from close range but spent much of the game complaining in referee Sam Barrott's ear - City team-mates and supporters may be expecting more from their club record signing.

The former Chelsea player scored in the midweek Champions League win at RB Leipzig, but that is his only goal or assist in his past nine games.

Maresca needs to work out how to get the best out of Fernandez during the international break.

Stone added: "I came here tonight thinking City would win, I thought they had chances. This is a real hammer blow to them, there is something not right about the back four at the minute.

"I have never seen a City team give the ball away so much in the middle of the park."

Rayan Cherki's stunning strike gave City hope but they could not turn it around and the numbers following the result make for grim:

City have lost three consecutive Premier League games for the first time since a run of four in November-December 2024

They have become the second team in English top-flight history - after Sheffield Wednesday in 1904-05 - to win their first seven games of a season and then lose their next three

This was their first league defeat by two or more goals against a side starting the day in the relegation zone since November 2008 (a 2-0 loss to Bolton Wanderers).

Maresca was forced to chop and change his defence again, withdrawing both Gvardiol and Marc Guehi at half-time because of injuries, according to the manager.

It meant Nunes came in at right-back, with Abdukodir Khusanov moving inside, and Nico O'Reilly playing down the left.

Former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy told BBC Sport: "I thought City's performance was poor in terms of mentality.

"To make so make so many mistakes when you go anywhere in the Premier League, but especially to a team who are fighting for the lives, and you know they're going to come after you.

"They were sloppy with the ball, not winning duels. I would even probably go as far as saying there was probably a bit of arrogance at the start of the game from them.

"I think that there are now some big questions to ask the manager about how he gets them back on track. I think with the talent they have got, it is not going to be a big problem.

"But I think defensively, maybe sticking to the same backline for a little while is the way forward."

#769. 'The worst conditions in my 35-year career' - commentating in the FA Cup fog

Notts County beat Altrincham in incredible fog-filled spectacle

One of the most important attributes for a commentator is to be able to see the action you are trying to describe but that became a luxury for BBC Sport's Steve Bower when Altrincham hosted Notts County in an FA Cup tie on Saturday.

As thick fog enveloped the Moss Lane ground, he could barely see what was going on in a first-round game being televised live on BBC Two.

"One of the more challenging of my long career, that's about 35 years now," said Bower about the experience.

"I was reminded by a colleague - maybe I'm a jinx - that we had a similar thing on the BBC about three years ago when we did York against Wigan in the second round and the fog came in.

"Tonight was worse. From where we were, opposite the dugouts, once the play went to the centre circle and beyond, we couldn't see a thing.

"We couldn't see which team had the ball, let alone which player had the ball after about the 60th minute. Bearing in mind it went to extra-time, it was challenging.

"I just kept looking down at my phone and it was text message after text message from people saying, 'You're sounding great, but I can't see a thing'. In the end, you have to roll with it and do the best you can."

Notts County progress in FA Cup tie no-one could see

'It's like a fever dream' - commentators struggle through fog

National League Altrincham were on for an upset when they took a 2-1 lead against the League One side but a late Callum Roberts equaliser for County took the game to extra-time before the visiting side won on penalties.

"The frustrating thing is that for an hour it was a really good FA Cup tie, it had everything," said Bower.

"It was on for another giant-killing script but then the frustrating thing is that it becomes a non-event because, without stating the obvious, people can't see half of it.

"Also, it's not then about the tactics, or the shape of it, or the aggression, or the effort because you just can't see it. As a spectacle in trying to describe a game like you normally would, it's impossible."

Bower's radio colleagues were not faring much better as they tried to work out what was going on.

"I can just about see the bright white numbers on their shirts, but I am struggling to see what is happening on the far side of the pitch," said BBC Radio Nottingham commentator Adam Hassell.

Former Notts County striker Mark Stallard, who was also speaking on BBC Radio Nottingham, said: "We're looking around, and here in the press box no-one knows where the ball is! It's like a spot-the-ball competition.

"I played in the Notts County cup side against Wimbledon when it was abandoned - they equalised in the second half and I didn't see any of it!"

Stallard later said: "We genuinely cannot see the linesman or the players on the far side. It's slightly farcical having to commentate for radio listeners."

Altrincham have a rich history of causing FA Cup upsets but could not add to that in the fog against Notts County

The managers of both teams were on the touchline but even they were struggling as tactics went out of the window.

"[Notts County boss] Martin Paterson said credit to Altrincham, they were the better team in the first half and, as for the second, I couldn't see it. He was laughing," said Bower.

"Neil Gibson, the Altrincham manager, was saying, 'We were trying to get down to pitchside to look tactically at what they had done after those four substitutions. Have they changed shape? Is it a back four? Have they gone to a box midfield? But we just couldn't see'.

"So even from a tactical point of view, the players had to stop playing long diagonal passes and things like that because they couldn't see, they were just having to play short five, 10 yard passes so the game changed in that sense as well.

"It was very, very close to getting called off."

Bower said some of the players told him they couldn't see both goals or the corner flags from the centre circle.

"It will live long in the memory, that's for sure," said Bower. "Even on the penalties, you were having to rely on the crowd's reaction before committing to the tale.

"You couldn't see the goalkeeper's save, for instance, until the first replay came in."

The penalties took place in front of Altrincham fans and, while Bower had replays to call on, the Notts County fans "couldn't have seen anything" from the other end as they had to go on "crowd reaction".

"Obviously, the Altrincham fans all had their phones on with the lights trying to put the Notts County players off as well in the fog. A unique evening all around."

#768. ‘Mathematics is more than a mechanical process’ — why I think the field will survive OpenAI’s disruption

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Ursula Martin is an emeritus professor at the Mathematical Institute, University of Oxford, UK.

In early October, the artificial-intelligence firm OpenAI posted more than 700 AI-generated mathematical manuscripts on an online public repository. The arguments — if found to be correct after verification — contain an extraordinary trove of new mathematical knowledge. The reaction to these developments from the maths community has ranged from exhilaration to despair. Some researchers worry they have spent their lifetimes attempting to solve problems and their work might now suddenly seem meaningless. Others have expressed concern about the negative impact on young colleagues who are entering the field during a period of flux. And there’s been widespread anger at the manner in which AI companies are releasing such findings.

As one of the authors of the Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics, which was published in June, I think some of the field’s concerns over OpenAI’s approach to announcing its discoveries could have been anticipated. In our declaration, we did not oppose the use of AI but put forwards several practical safeguards. These included the need for clear citation policies, precise disclosures on how AI is used and a renewed commitment to the long-standing expectation that all arguments made in a maths proof should be independently verifiable and answerable by a human author. Some AI companies have agreed to follow the declaration. OpenAI has not.

Mathematicians are developing rules for AI use — other fields should follow

Mathematicians are developing rules for AI use — other fields should follow

Now that mathematicians have started analysing the AI-assisted proofs, it’s clear that many of the 700 preprints are presented in a sloppy, rough-and-ready style, making them hard to understand. The inner workings of OpenAI’s closed models are unknown, and there is also no human author named who might take responsibility for explaining or correcting the content if flaws emerge. It will take mathematicians a lot of time and effort to check the work in the preprints and rewrite it in a professional format that is suitable for judgement by peer reviewers. Unsurprisingly, many mathematicians are unenthusiastic about clearing up OpenAI’s mess, however exciting the underlying mathematics might be.

So, what does this mean for the future of mathematics? Creatively rethinking how the field must evolve will require action at every level. Outstanding leadership by individuals such as mathematician Terence Tao, and grassroots initiatives such as the Leiden declaration, need to be complemented with high-level engagement from stakeholder institutions such as the International Mathematical Union. It would be a disservice to the field if AI companies are allowed to set the norms on how to do mathematics without wide-ranging input from academics.

#767. 'I can't believe he is one of us' - inside Salah's life in Trabzon

Mohamed Salah has scored 10 goals in 15 games for Turkish club Trabzonspor

Back in August, when Mohamed Salah landed in Istanbul after flying in from his holiday in Mykonos, he wore Trabzonspor's burgundy and blue home strip as he stepped out of the plane to be greeted by thousands of fans.

That kit sold out almost instantly. Later that day, as Salah headed to Trabzon in north-east Turkey to complete the formalities of one of the most unexpected transfers after the expiry of his Liverpool contract, he asked one of his entourage what he should wear.

"The same kit," came the response, but Trabzonspor president Ertugrul Dogan advised Salah to wear the black away kit instead. Of course, that sold out too.

From the outset of the 34-year-old's arrival to this historic port city on the Black Sea, that sense of adulation has only grown.

"I went to the airport to see him in Istanbul and it was surreal," says Nisa Dumangoz. "I still can't believe that he is one of us."

Go for a stroll through Trabzon on matchday and it is Salah's face which adorns everything. Even the walls inside the fishmongers have pictures of him.

At the club shop in town, one of the staff jokes that the ground floor is for the Egyptian and the upper floor is for everything else.

Outside the stadium, there are scarves, magnets, keyrings, lighters with his face on and Egyptian Nemes headdresses in Trabzonspor colours. Season ticket sales rocketed after his arrival.

"Walking around Trabzon, it feels as though nine out of every 10 fans wearing a shirt have Salah's name on the back. The 10th has their own," says Turkish football journalist Hasan Tuncel.

The club have surpassed their merchandise revenue from last year in three months since Salah's arrival, while the local airport is only getting busier.

Liverpool was difficult to reach for many supporters across the Arab world and tickets were often hard to source. Trabzon is far more accessible, with new flights introduced from Cairo, Dubai and Riyadh since Salah's arrival.

On our flight from Istanbul, we meet an Egyptian family of 10 coming from Cairo for Trabzonspor's Uefa Conference League game against Freiburg.

"He is our ambassador and our Egyptian King, and with how many people want to come to Turkey now, he is their ambassador too," says Mahmoud.

At the game, there is a group of Egyptian celebrities and influencers. A quick check of their social media shows their combined Instagram following of about five million. Trabzonspor have three million. Salah has 68 million.

Salah recently went for a hike and posed for a picture on a rock in the Trabzon highlands. That rock has been renamed Salahtasi (Salah's Rock) and is now a tourist destination.

The commercial element of his signing has more than been justified but crucially, on the pitch, Salah is driving Trabzonspor's push for the Turkish Super Lig title and he has hit the ground running with 10 goals and five assists in all competitions.

Trabzonspor trail leaders Galatasaray by three points, having won seven of their first 10 games, including victories against the table-toppers and Besiktas.

For context, the Istanbul 'big three' of Galatasaray (26), Fenerbahce (19) and Besiktas (16) have won the league on 61 occasions combined, compared with Trabzonspor's seven titles.

"In Turkey, he is the biggest football star after Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo," says Kerim Tonyali, who is part of Gurbetci Gencler, a Trabzonspor supporters' group.

And given Salah's status as an icon, Trabzonspor are quickly becoming the second club for many in Turkey and the wider Muslim world.

Salah's face is a common sight wherever you go in Trabzon

Trabzon may be more than 2,000 miles from Liverpool but there are similarities, particularly when it comes to the sense of identity and pride associated with originating from here.

"Everywhere is Trabzon for us," is the local mantra and aligns with the sense of unity within this city that has a population of about 800,000 and is only the 30th-biggest in Turkey.

For Salah, the financials were important and he is earning about Â£14.6m per year as well as 20% of official merchandise sold with his name on, but one of the key aspects of coming here was the ability to focus entirely on his football.

Besiktas was considered as an option after the 2026 World Cup but, after multiple calls with Trabzonspor, Salah felt they were the ideal fit and offered a life away from the hustle and bustle of Istanbul.

He has his own security detail and is living in the nearby town of Yomra, where he now has a street named after him. He also employs a private chef and, unsurprisingly, continues to set standards in the gym and on the training ground.

By all accounts, Salah is thriving. He is a fan of Turkish coffee and is often spotted leaving the ground with Ayran - a traditional yogurt drink - but as much as he wants to explore the city, he knows of the difficulties given his reputation.

"Everyone wants to work with a star like Mohamed Salah," said Trabzonspor's Paul Onuachu, formerly of Southampton. "He adds so much and helps all of us and he contributes positively. I am grateful for him. It's a blessing to play with him."

Watching Salah in the flesh in a Conference League game against Freiburg, his pace has gone down a notch compared with his peak but the touch, quick feet and sheer quality is still there. And so is that knack of getting in goalscoring positions, even if his defensive duties - which were such a source of debate last season at Liverpool - are limited.

Salah believes he still has plenty to give for club and country, with aspirations to play in both the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations and 2030 World Cup, which will be partly held in North Africa.

No decision has been made about how long he will stay in Turkey, but there is growing belief among sources in the Middle East that he will move to Saudi Arabia when his two-year Trabzonspor deal expires in 2028. By then, he will be 36.

Salah signed a two-year deal with Trabzonspor in the summer of 2026

On initial thoughts, it is easy to question how and why Salah ended up here.

When he delivered that infamous mixed-zone interview at Leeds' Elland Road less than a year ago and the wheels of his departure from Liverpool were set in motion, surely no-one would have imagined his next destination would be this Turkish outpost near the Georgian border.

"I remember looking at him when we landed in Trabzon and seeing the crowds outside and how emotional it was," says Anil Dincer, one of the lawyers involved in Salah's move to Turkey.

"We already have Salah and Fabinho. So now we are waiting for [Virgil] Van Dijk," adds Serhat Sumer, a Trabzonspor fan.

Salah, of course, delivered so much joy to Liverpool and the intention here is the same. This is no drift towards retirement, but a player determined to prove he still belongs at the highest level and that football still has meaning beyond trophies and money.

Asked by BBC Sport if he had a message for Liverpool fans, Salah simply said "hello" and smiled. Given how rarely he spoke in the mixed zone during his time at Anfield, it is not in his nature to talk regularly on record.

Last season was Salah's least prolific at Anfield, but given Liverpool's struggles in front of goal in the Premier League, it is hard to argue they have replaced one of their greatest ever players.

Perhaps a time will come when the likes of Salah, Arne Slot and Richard Hughes will reveal more about the chain of events that led to the forward agreeing to terminate his contract a year early. As it is, none of them are at the club and that chapter is firmly closed.

Salah's influence that once helped shape the Premier League is now being felt on the shores of the Black Sea. He is Trabzonspor's force of nature. And the team known as the Black Sea Storm are rising and on the hunt for silverware with their Egyptian King.

A rock in the Trabzon highlands became a tourist destination after Salah's visit

#766. Benson Boone Brings Young Fan Battling Cancer Onstage at Brisbane Concert

"I've had the opportunity of meeting a 13-year-old girl who is battling her second round of cancer," Boone told the crowd.

Benson Boone opened the Australian leg of his Wanted Man tour with a special guest. He brought a 13-year-old fan who is battling cancer onstage to sing “Beautiful Things” with him on her birthday. Explore Benson Boone See latest videos, charts and news

The moment came at the end of Boone’s set at Brisbane Entertainment Centre on Friday (Nov. 6). The Music reported that the singer stopped to introduce the final song. Related Deep Purple's Ian Gillan Shares Encouraging News After Undergoing Surgery Richard Lloyd, Television Guitarist, Dies at 75 Céline Dion Plays Air Bass at Metallica's Sphere Show

“I’ve had the opportunity of meeting a 13-year-old girl who is battling her second round of cancer,” Boone told the crowd, according to the outlet. “It’s her birthday today and her birthday wish was to come on stage and sing ‘Beautiful Things.’”

The fan, Kenzie Riddle, then rose from an upper platform and joined Boone on the song. According to The Music, roughly 10,000 people were in the arena.

Riddle has Ewing’s sarcoma. As reported by Nine’s Today, she believed she had beaten the illness after about two and a half years of treatment, but the cancer returned and she is now facing intensive chemotherapy. Her family said they bought tickets to the show in July as her 13th birthday present. Her campaign to meet Boone took off online after a local musician, Fergus Hogan, shared an Instagram video about her story.

“I love his energetic style and how he’s so over the top,” Riddle told Today before the concert. “He’s kinda crazy and I love it.”

Her family also told the program: “She’s such an unbelievable inspiration to so many people… But I think even bigger than that is the community behind her.”

“Beautiful Things” was Boone’s breakout single. Released in January 2024, it reached No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 and became one of the most-streamed songs in the world that year. Boone followed it with his debut album Fireworks & Rollerblades that April. His second album, American Heart, arrived in 2025 and included the single “Mystical Magical.”

The Brisbane show opened Boone’s Wanted Man tour of Australia. Boone has two additional Brisbane performances scheduled for Nov. 7 and 8 before the tour heads to Melbourne for three concerts at Rod Laver Arena beginning Nov. 12. The Australian leg concludes with three shows at Sydney’s Afterpay Arena from Nov. 17-19.

#765. Gen Z protests in Germany: Is France-style violence looming?

Young people in Germany are preparing to protest over education and climate change. Politicians fear violence like in France, but an expert sees differences.

As politicians in Germany look ahead to the coming weekend, many fear that cities across the country could witness the kind of violent unrest that recently shook France. An initiative known as "Gen Z regelt" ("Gen Z sorts it") has launched a social media campaign calling for demonstrations in 23 cities nationwide.

"Gen Z" broadly refers to the generation born between 1995 and 2010. Many feel that their parents' generation has done too little to combat climate change and has allowed the gap between rich and poor to widen ever further. At the same time, they are concerned about their educational prospects and future opportunities.

In France, what began as largely peaceful protests recently spiraled into serious unrest. Cars were set alight in several towns, while in Limoges the town hall was torched. In Lille, Lyon, and Toulouse and elsewhere, police deployed tear gas, leading to numerous arrests.

Many politicians, particularly within Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), are warning of similar scenes this coming weekend.

Alexander Throm, the CDU parliamentary group's domestic spokesperson, told the daily Handelsblatt newspaper: "Scenes like those in France must be prevented at all costs."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Throm's view, far-left groups and criminals from immigrant communities could "hijack" the demonstrations. "An ominous alliance is emerging, particularly in Berlin," he warned.

Marc Henrichmann, also of the CDU, chair of the Bundestag's parliamentary oversight panel for the intelligence services, also expressed concern: "The far-left extremist scene is internationally connected and coordinated." He said that violent far-left activists now even cross national borders to engage in looting and acts of violence elsewhere.

But Sebastian Koos, sociologist at the University of Konstanz whose research focuses on youth and protest movements, told DW that he does not expect Germany to experience unrest on a scale comparable to that seen in France, even though events in the neighboring country helped spark the protests now being planned across Germany.

Koos sees key differences between young people in the two countries. "Unlike in France, these protests are not driven by the same level of anger," he said. "They have been planned, officially registered and carefully organized. The website, in particular, places strong emphasis on peaceful protest and repeatedly stresses a non-violent approach."

At the same time, the sociologist does not rule out the possibility that extremist groups could exploit the authorized demonstrations to stir up unrest: "It is certainly very important for the police and public authorities to be well prepared."

Quentin Gärtner, 19, studies biotechnology in Heidelberg and served until November of last year as secretary-general of the Federal Student Conference, which represents around 7.5 million school students in Germany.

"What unites us is that we have run out of patience with the education system. Many young people are deeply frustrated," he told DW. "The performance of German school students continues to decline, teaching positions are constantly being cut, and in many cases school buildings have seen little or no meaningful investment for years."

For Gärtner, the discontent reflects a broader problem with parliamentary democracy in Germany and many other Western countries.

"Politicians want to win elections. They focus on the groups that matter most to them electorally rather than on the future and the long-term sustainability of their policies," he said.

"And in our aging societies, older people and the baby boomer generation are the groups that carry the most political weight."

Opposition parties in Germany have also voiced understanding for the concerns of younger people. Speaking to Germany's public broadcaster ZDF, Green Party co-leader Felix Banaszak said: "The intergenerational contract is no longer working. Older generations have driven the climate into a dead end."

He argued that the social welfare system was also reaching its limits and that rents had become unaffordable. According to Banaszak, the only thing the state seems to offer young people are the letters sent to 18-year-olds asking them to consider joining the military. Germany is currently desperate to expand the Bundeswehr and is considering reintroducing national service.

By Tuesday, around 134,000 people had registered on the "Gen Z regelt" website to take part in the protests planned for the coming Saturday. With several days still to go before the demonstrations, that number could rise further.
