#615. Scientists discover that a clogged filter could revolutionize oil refining

Researchers have developed a surprisingly simple way to separate crude oil without heating it, potentially transforming one of the world's most energy-intensive industrial processes. The breakthrough uses an inexpensive membrane that could significantly reduce the energy required for oil refining while lowering operating costs and carbon emissions.

The international research effort was led by Professor Dong-Yeun Koh at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, known as KAIST, in collaboration with Professor Ryan Lively's research group at Georgia Tech. KAIST(President Kwang Hyung Lee) announced that the team had successfully demonstrated a membrane capable of separating crude oil at room temperature. The findings were published in Nature, one of the world's leading scientific journals.

Crude oil is essential for far more than gasoline and other transportation fuels. It also supplies the raw materials used to manufacture plastics, packaging, clothing, and numerous everyday products. Because refining costs affect the prices of these materials, making the process more efficient could have widespread economic and environmental benefits.

Why Traditional Crude Oil Refining Requires So Much Energy

For more than a century, oil refineries have relied heavily on distillation to separate crude oil into useful components. The process involves heating oil to temperatures above 350 °C, turning portions of it into vapor, and then cooling those vapors to collect different fractions.

This approach requires an enormous amount of energy. Worldwide, crude oil distillation consumes approximately 1,100 terawatt-hours (TWh) annually. That is comparable to the combined yearly electricity production of roughly 130 continuously operating nuclear power plants, each with a capacity of about one gigawatt.

The massive energy demand makes distillation a major contributor to both fuel consumption and greenhouse gas emissions within the refining industry. Meanwhile, growing economic pressures across global petrochemical markets have increased interest in technologies that can separate oil more efficiently.

Membranes have emerged as a promising alternative because they can separate substances without requiring the extreme temperatures used in conventional distillation. However, previous designs have faced significant obstacles.

Traditionally, researchers have assumed that effective molecular separation requires a membrane covered with an extremely thin, specialized coating. Although these coatings can provide the necessary precision, they are expensive to produce and can develop defects when manufactured on a large scale. These limitations have made widespread industrial adoption difficult.

A Surprising Discovery Turns Clogged Filters Into an Advantage

The KAIST and Georgia Tech researchers approached the problem differently. Rather than adding a complicated coating, they used a bare membrane made from porous polyacrylonitrile (PAN), an inexpensive, chemically stable polymer already commonly used as a supporting material in industrial filtration systems.

What happened when crude oil passed through the membrane was unexpected.

As the oil flowed through its pores, heavier hydrocarbon molecules accumulated along the inner walls. This buildup gradually reduced the size of the openings, producing extremely narrow channels measuring less than 2 nanometers across.

In effect, the crude oil helped create the microscopic pathways needed to separate its own components.

These naturally formed channels allowed lighter oil fractions, including naphtha, gasoline, and kerosene, to pass through quickly while preventing heavier substances from traveling through the membrane as easily.

The discovery was especially surprising because the buildup of material inside membrane pores, known as fouling, is normally considered a serious problem. Fouling typically reduces filtration performance and requires cleaning or replacement. In this case, however, the same phenomenon made the membrane highly effective at separating different molecules.

The results were impressive. The uncoated PAN membrane achieved crude oil permeation rates approximately 23 times higher than those reported for previous leading crude oil separation membranes. It also continued operating with stable performance for 28 consecutive days.

Professor Ryan Lively (Georgia Tech) commented: "One of the key challenges facing membrane systems for crude oil separation was the low productivities of the membrane units -- the PAN membranes with their surprising separation mechanism -- dramatically increase the productivity of the membrane unit, to the point where industry should seriously consider adopting the technology."

New Membrane Could Cut Oil Refining Energy Use by Nearly a Third

One of the technology's biggest advantages is that refineries would not necessarily need to replace their existing equipment to use it.

The membrane could instead be installed as a modular filtration system that processes crude oil before it enters conventional distillation equipment. This would reduce the amount of work required during the heating and separation stages while allowing facilities to continue using much of their current infrastructure.

Computer simulations suggest that incorporating the membrane into the refining process could deliver substantial improvements. Energy consumption could fall by 31.6%, while carbon dioxide emissions could decrease by 37.6%. The same calculations projected a 20.7% reduction in cooling water consumption and a 36% decrease in operating costs.

The potential environmental benefits could be considerable if the technology were adopted widely.

Researchers estimate that implementing the system throughout Korea's refining and petrochemical industries could prevent approximately 10 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions each year. That is roughly equivalent to the annual emissions produced by four million vehicles powered by internal combustion engines.

These savings are projections based on process simulations rather than reductions already demonstrated across operating refineries. Nevertheless, the findings suggest that membrane filtration could become a practical way to improve the efficiency of existing facilities.

Although crude oil separation was the main focus of the research, the same technology could eventually be useful in several other industries.

One potential application involves treating pyrolysis oil produced when waste plastics are broken down for recycling. The membranes could also help recover solvents used in battery manufacturing, purify pharmaceutical compounds, and improve biofuel production.

The broader opportunity lies in using complex liquid mixtures to help form the tiny filtration channels needed to separate their components. This approach could provide a more affordable and versatile alternative to conventional membranes that require precisely manufactured surface coatings.

Professor Dong-Yeun Koh of KAIST said, "This study reveals a new scientific principle in which a membrane interacts with a complex mixture and spontaneously forms its own separation channels. Working with real crude oil supplied by HD Hyundai Oilbank allowed us to validate the technology under conditions relevant to industrial operation."

The use of actual crude oil was an important part of the research because it allowed the team to examine how the membrane performed with the complicated mixture of hydrocarbons found in industrial feedstocks.

Before the technology can be deployed more widely, the researchers plan to improve membrane production at larger scales and establish its reliability during extended operation.

Professor Jae W. Lee of KAIST, a co-corresponding author of the study, added, "By advancing large-area membrane modularization and long-term operational reliability, we hope to broaden the adoption of membrane-based processes throughout the refining and petrochemical industries."

Dr. Jihoon Choi and Dr. Hyeokjun Seo of KAIST, the study's co-first authors, said, "Our goal is to precisely control this spontaneous pore-constriction phenomenon and develop it into a membrane platform applicable to the entire refining process. We also aim to expand the technology to plastic recycling, biofuel purification, and other sustainable chemical processes that support carbon neutrality."

The research received support from Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT through the Basic Research Program for Outstanding Early-Career Researchers and the Engineering Research Center (ERC) Program.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Another new private rocket is in the works.

AST SpaceMobile announced today (Nov. 6) that it's building a reusable rocket called Blacklift to launch its broadband satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO), with first flight targeted in 2028.

The news comes just 10 days after Cowboy Space unveiled Big Iron, a rocket designed to launch its constellation of 20,000 AI data centers. Cowboy Space is also targeting 2028 for its first liftoff.

"The Blacklift rocket is the springboard to significantly expand our total addressable market, providing AST SpaceMobile with regular unconstrained access to orbit and providing for most favorable owners’ economics in the industry," Abel Avellan, the company's founder, chairman and CEO, said in a statement today.

"This will accelerate our mission to build a new layer of global connectivity, extending connectivity beyond terrestrial networks and helping to bring AI-enabled services wherever people live, work and travel," Avellan added.

Texas-based AST SpaceMobile is building a LEO constellation composed of its BlueBird satellites, which beam internet service directly to cell phones. The company has launched 13 BlueBirds to date, including eight "Block 2" variants. The antennas on each of these next-gen spacecraft cover a whopping 2,400 square feet (223 square m) — the largest ever deployed in LEO by a commercial satellite.

BlueBirds have flown atop three different rockets to date — SpaceX's Falcon 9, Blue Origin's New Glenn and India's Launch Vehicle Mark-3. But AST SpaceMobile wants to get more vertically integrated, which explains the push to develop Blacklift.

The company won't be starting from scratch. It has signed a deal with another Texas-based outfit, Firefly Aerospace, to provide the engines (and associated engineering services) for the first three Blacklift launches. After that, AST SpaceMobile will build the engines itself, under a licensing agreement with Firefly.

Those engines are Miranda, which will power Blacklift's booster, and Vira, which will power the upper stage.

Neither engine has flight experience. (Firefly's currently operational rocket, Alpha, uses Reavers in its booster and Lightnings in its upper stage.) But Miranda has been tested extensively on the ground, firing for more than 4,200 seconds over the course of 175 hot fires, according to AST SpaceMobile.

"The Miranda engine will allow us to leapfrog the traditional five-to-10-year development cycle as we build Blacklift," AST SpaceMobile President Scott Wisniewski said in the same statement.

The "supply and services" agreement for the first three launches is worth $500 million. The licensing agreement cost AST SpaceMobile about $800 million, with half of that paid in cash and half in stock, according to the statement.

Blacklift will be able to haul 20 tons to LEO. Each launch will therefore be able to loft up to five BlueBird satellites, according to today's announcement. (For perspective: The Falcon 9's LEO lift capacity is about 25 tons.)

BlueBirds will continue going up while AST SpaceMobile gets Blacklift ready to fly: The company already holds contracts with other providers to launch more than 100 of the satellites over the course of 2027 and 2028.

The launch landscape will likely be very different when Blacklift, Big Iron and other new rockets come online. SpaceX has said that it plans to phase out the Falcon 9, as well as its Falcon Heavy heavy lifter, after its Starship megarocket gets up and running.

That milestone could come in the next few years, ushering in something of a launch crunch for satellite operators. SpaceX has indicated that it will prioritize launches of its own satellites with Starship. And there will be a lot of them to loft — 100,000 Starlink V3 satellites and a million Starmind AI data centers, company founder and CEO Elon Musk has suggested.

#612. New photo reveals an asteroid view that a NASA spacecraft never saw

Europe's Hera spacecraft just took its first close-up picture of Didymos and Dimorphos, the asteroid pair NASA used for target practice in 2022.

The European Space Agency mission is designed to do a sort of crash scene investigation following NASA's DART mission, the first planetary defense rehearsal. DART, which stands for Double Asteroid Redirection Test, involved sending a 1,300-pound, refrigerator-size spacecraft straight for Dimorphos, the smaller asteroid orbiting Didymos, to see if a strike could change its trajectory in space.

The spacecraft's hip check to Dimorphos seems to have worked, lopping 33 minutes off its orbit. But the change was more significant than scientists predicted, leaving open questions on the extent of the impact and why it unfolded the way it did.

The new black-and-white photo shows Didymos, which measures about a half-mile wide, from about 37 miles away. Shadow hides most of Dimorphos, its 500-foot-wide battered moonlet.

Hera's view shows the side of Didymos that NASA's spacecraft never saw before the crash. The "backside" looks remarkably different, according to the team, with boulders, craters, and grooves. It also shows the continuation of a ridge that wraps around the asteroid's middle.

"The first thing we said was 'Wow!'" said Patrick Michel, Hera's principal investigator, in a statement. "This feels like looking at a whole new world."

Some of these features may come from debris the crash blasted across the half-mile gap between Dimorphos and Didymos, said mission scientist Michael Kueppers. The space agency will release detailed images of both asteroids on Nov. 25.

The robotic spacecraft, about the size of a small car, flew for two years to reach the asteroids, which now sit about 122 million miles from Earth.

Scientists hope Hera's findings will help turn "kinetic impact" — ramming a spacecraft into an asteroid to nudge it — from a one-time experiment into a reliable planetary defense tool, if Earth ever needs it.

Want more science and tech news delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for Mashable's Top Stories newsletter today.

When DART hit, it blasted rock and dust into space, and that spray pushed the asteroid like a rocket's exhaust. Scientists call this extra kickback the "beta factor," and Hera will help measure it. That number could tell future mission planners how hard they'd need to punch a killer asteroid (unlike Dimorphos, which posed no threat) to move it out of Earth's way.

But before scientists can answer that, Hera has to see what DART left behind. The spacecraft will map the crash site to learn whether the collision caused a deep crater, left a shallow dent, or changed the asteroid's whole shape.

Scientists also want to know if the impact knocked Dimorphos into a wobble. Before the crash, Dimorphos always kept the same face toward its larger partner, the way our moon does with Earth. Telescope data now hint that it may be tumbling.

Hera's small companion probe, Juventas, will scan the interior with radar, sort of like taking an X-ray, to look inside the asteroid. Meanwhile, Hera will measure the asteroid's mass and density to show how tightly it's packed. Dimorphos might be a single solid rock, or it might be a loose pile of boulders with empty gaps between them.

Its composition could explain why it reacted the way it did during the collision. Gravity on Dimorphos is about 200,000 times weaker than on Earth, so even the tiny forces that make particles stick together could affect how the asteroid holds up under a hit.

"We have an exciting work ahead of us to sort it out," Kueppers said. "We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify."

#611. AI helps Stanford scientists discover a “natural Ozempic” with a surprising advantage

Scientists at Stanford Medicine have identified a naturally occurring molecule that could lead to a new generation of weight loss medications. Early animal experiments suggest that it can suppress appetite and promote fat loss much like semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic, while potentially avoiding some of the drug's troublesome side effects.

The molecule, known as BRP, works differently from existing treatments. Rather than affecting several organs throughout the body, it appears to act more selectively on a part of the brain responsible for controlling hunger and metabolism. This more focused approach could eventually help people lose weight without experiencing problems such as nausea, constipation, or substantial muscle loss.

Researchers discovered BRP with the help of artificial intelligence, which allowed them to search through thousands of possible biological compounds. The findings were promising enough that the scientists began preparing for the next major step: determining whether the molecule is safe and effective in humans.

"The receptors targeted by semaglutide are found in the brain but also in the gut, pancreas and other tissues," said assistant professor of pathology Katrin Svensson, PhD. "That's why Ozempic has widespread effects including slowing the movement of food through the digestive tract and lowering blood sugar levels. In contrast, BRP appears to act specifically in the hypothalamus, which controls appetite and metabolism."

The hypothalamus is a small but essential region deep within the brain. Among its many responsibilities, it helps regulate hunger, energy use, body temperature, and other functions needed to maintain the body's internal balance. Because it plays such a central role in appetite, it is an important target for researchers developing obesity treatments.

Semaglutide works by imitating a hormone called glucagon-like peptide 1, or GLP-1. This hormone helps regulate blood sugar and signals that influence hunger and feelings of fullness. However, GLP-1 receptors are distributed throughout several parts of the body, which helps explain why medications that activate them can produce effects beyond appetite suppression.

BRP appears to take another route. Although it influences some of the same broad metabolic functions as semaglutide, it activates different populations of brain cells. Scientists believe this distinction could make it possible to control hunger more precisely while reducing unwanted effects elsewhere in the body.

Svensson, who served as senior author of the study, published in Nature, has also cofounded a company to advance BRP toward human clinical trials. The research was led by senior research scientist Laetitia Coassolo, PhD.

How Artificial Intelligence Uncovered a Hidden Molecule

Finding BRP required solving a problem that has long complicated the search for new hormones. The human body produces enormous numbers of small protein fragments, but only a fraction have important biological functions. Identifying the ones that influence appetite or metabolism can be extremely difficult.

Many hormones begin as larger, inactive proteins known as prohormones. Specialized enzymes cut these proteins into smaller pieces called peptides. Some of those peptides become chemical messengers that help coordinate processes such as energy metabolism, appetite, and organ function.

A single prohormone can be cut in several different places, potentially producing numerous peptides with distinct effects. The challenge is determining which fragments are biologically useful and which are simply leftovers from normal protein processing. The important peptide hormones (which are relatively rare) can be difficult to distinguish from the much larger collection of ordinary protein fragments.

Traditional approaches often involve extracting proteins from biological tissues and analyzing them with techniques such as mass spectrometry. This method identifies molecules by measuring characteristics related to their mass, but the sheer number of possible peptides makes searching for new hormones a demanding process.

The Stanford team decided to approach the problem differently. They concentrated on an enzyme called prohormone convertase 1/3, which cuts prohormones at particular amino acid sequences and has previously been linked to human obesity. Amino acids are the molecular building blocks of proteins, and their arrangement helps determine where enzymes can cut them.

One of the hormones produced through this process is GLP-1, the same hormone whose effects semaglutide mimics. The researchers reasoned that other peptides generated through similar processing might also help regulate appetite and energy use.

AI Searches 20,000 Human Genes for New Hormones

To accelerate the search, the scientists created a computer algorithm called Peptide Predictor. Instead of physically isolating and examining hundreds of thousands of peptides, the program analyzed the roughly 20,000 genes that encode human proteins, looking for sequences where the enzyme was likely to make cuts.

The team then refined the results by concentrating on genes associated with proteins released outside cells, a common characteristic of hormones. They also required each candidate protein to contain at least four potential cutting sites.

These filters reduced an enormous collection of possibilities to 373 prohormones, making experimental testing much more practical.

"The algorithm was absolutely key to our findings," Svensson said.

Peptide Predictor estimated that the enzyme could produce 2,683 distinct peptides from those 373 proteins. From this collection, Svensson and Coassolo selected candidates that appeared particularly likely to influence brain activity.

The researchers eventually tested 100 peptides, including GLP-1, using nerve cells grown in the laboratory. Their goal was to find substances capable of stimulating neuronal activity, an early indication that a peptide might influence important brain processes.

A Tiny Peptide Produces a Surprising Result

GLP-1 performed strongly in the laboratory tests, increasing neuronal activity to three times the level observed in untreated control cells.

One previously unrecognized peptide, however, produced an even more striking response. Consisting of just 12 amino acids, it increased neuronal activity tenfold compared with the controls.

The researchers named the molecule BRP after the larger protein from which it originates, BPM/retinoic acid inducible neural specific 2, or BRINP2 (BRINP2-related-peptide).

That unusually powerful response made BRP a promising candidate for further investigation. The next question was whether stimulating laboratory-grown brain cells would translate into meaningful changes in appetite and body weight in living animals.

Food Intake Drops by Up to 50% in Animal Experiments

The team tested BRP in lean mice and minipigs (which more closely mirror human metabolism and eating patterns than mice do). Before the animals were fed, researchers administered BRP through an injection into the muscle.

The results were striking. During the following hour, the treated animals consumed up to 50% less food than expected, suggesting that BRP could strongly influence hunger.

The scientists then examined whether repeated treatment could produce sustained changes in body weight. Obese mice received daily BRP injections for 14 days. By the end of the experiment, the treated mice had lost an average of 3 grams, while untreated control mice had gained approximately 3 grams.

Importantly, nearly all the weight lost by the BRP-treated mice came from body fat rather than muscle. Preserving muscle is an important goal in obesity treatment because muscle tissue supports strength, mobility, and metabolic health.

The treated animals also showed improvements in glucose and insulin tolerance. These measurements reflect how effectively the body handles sugar and responds to insulin, the hormone that helps move glucose from the bloodstream into cells.

Together, the findings suggest that BRP may influence both appetite and metabolic health, although it remains unknown whether people would experience comparable benefits.

Could BRP Avoid Common Ozempic Side Effects?

One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery is the possibility that BRP could provide weight loss benefits while avoiding some unwanted effects associated with semaglutide and similar medications.

To investigate potential side effects, the researchers monitored the behavior and physical responses of the treated mice and pigs. They found no significant differences in movement, water consumption, anxiety-related behavior, or fecal output compared with control animals.

The absence of changes in fecal production was particularly interesting because constipation is a known side effect of medications such as Ozempic. The experiments also showed that BRP promoted fat loss without the substantial muscle loss that can accompany some weight reduction treatments.

Nausea is another common concern with existing GLP-1 medications, although animal experiments cannot fully establish whether BRP would prevent that symptom in people. Human testing will be essential to determine the molecule's actual side effect profile.

Additional investigations into brain activity and other physiological responses reinforced the idea that BRP works differently from semaglutide. The peptide activated distinct neuronal and metabolic pathways rather than simply copying the effects of GLP-1.

This difference may explain why the researchers observed strong appetite suppression without several of the behavioral and digestive changes they were monitoring.

What Comes Next for the Potential Ozempic Alternative?

Despite the encouraging findings, BRP is still at an early stage of development. Researchers need to understand more about exactly how the molecule communicates with cells and how its effects might be sustained over longer periods.

One priority is identifying the cell surface receptors that recognize BRP. Receptors are specialized proteins that respond to particular chemical signals, allowing cells to detect messages and trigger appropriate biological responses. Determining which receptors BRP activates could help explain its effects on hunger and metabolism.

The team also wants to investigate ways of extending the molecule's activity inside the body. Peptides can be broken down relatively quickly, potentially requiring frequent injections. A longer-lasting version of BRP could make treatment more convenient if it eventually proves effective in people.

The ultimate challenge will be establishing whether its apparent advantages in animals translate into meaningful benefits for patients. Clinical trials will need to evaluate its safety, effectiveness, appropriate dosage, and potential side effects before it could become a practical obesity treatment.

"The lack of effective drugs to treat obesity in humans has been a problem for decades," Svensson said. "Nothing we've tested before has compared to semaglutide's ability to decrease appetite and body weight. We are very eager to learn if it is safe and effective in humans."

Scientists from the University of California, Berkeley; the University of Minnesota; and the University of British Columbia also participated in the research.

Financial support came from the National Institutes of Health (grants R01DK125260, P30DK116074, K99AR081618 and GM113854), the SPARK Translational Research Program at Stanford, Stanford Bio-X, the Stanford Maternal and Child Health Research Institute, the American Heart Association, a Stanford Medicine Dean's Fellowship Award, the Carlsberg Foundation, and the Wu Tsai Human Performance Alliance.

Svensson and Coassolo are named inventors on patents involving the use of BRP peptides to treat metabolic disorders. Svensson is also a cofounder of Merrifield Therapeutics.

"These observations were an important piece of evidence that the heavens were not immutable."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day.

Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star."

At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago. Because Tycho's Star is 13,000 light-years from Earth, it took a while before anyone could see it.

The Tycho supernova, known technically as SN 1572, is known today as a Type Ia supernova, which is a star explosion in a binary star system in which a white dwarf star draws material away from its partner, then explodes. But in 1572, the Tycho supernova appeared as something very different: a bright new star.

While Schulër was first, other astronomers also observed the apparently new star in the sky. Tycho Brahe's numerous observations are the most well known, in no small part becuause he wrote a book all about them in "De Stella Nova" (Latin for "On The New Star." At the time, the prevailing theory among scientists was that the stars were unchanging, yet here was a new star -- a changed sky.

"The 16th century exploding star, which appeared in the constellation Cassiopeia, was seen in daylight for about two weeks, and remained visible to the naked eye for 16 months," the University of California Berkeley wrote in 2004. "Brahe's meticulous record of the brightening and dimming of the supernova now allows astronomers to identify its 'light signature" as that of a Type Ia supernova."

"This was at the end of the Dark Ages in Europe, and these observations were an important piece of evidence that the heavens were not immutable," astronomer Alex Filippenko, who led a 2004 study on the origins of the Tycho supernova, said at the time.

Today, astronomers are closely watching another star that might explode. Called T Corona Borealis, or the Blaze Star, the object is expected to be on the verge of exploding in a nova (a star explosion that is smaller than a supernova and may not destroy the star). is one of 11 known stars observed to have recurring nova explosions within gaps of 100 years or so.

#609. How to play GTA 6 a day before everyone else in the U.S.

GTA fans have waited 13 years for Grand Theft Auto VI. Finally, the next installment of the GTA series comes out on Nov. 19.

There's no early access for GTA 6. You simply have to wait until the release date.

But what if you could play GTA 6 on Nov. 18? Or, more accurately, roughly 18 hours before everyone else in the U.S.? Well, there's a way to do just that.

GTA 6 will have a global release date, dropping at midnight for each time zone. This means that New Zealand, which is 18 hours ahead of Eastern Time in the U.S., will get to play the long-awaited game before everyone else.

If you have an Xbox, there's long been a not-so-secret trick on Xbox consoles that lets U.S.-based gamers access games a little bit before everyone else in the country.

As our friends at PCMag point out, gamers can simply go to their Xbox dashboard and do the following:

Select Language & Location on the right-hand side

Hit Restart Now to restart your console and save the settings

This has previously worked to access other games early, as it tricks the console into thinking it's on New Zealand time. It's possible that Microsoft switches things up and closes the loophole before the launch of GTA 6. But, as of now, unless anything changes, it should work.

This is a quick and easy process, and you'll be able to change the settings back on your Xbox the same way.

Also, be sure to pre-order the digital version of GTA 6 as you'll be able to download the game on Nov. 10. While it won't be playable until the release, it'll be ready to go on your console as soon as it does release without having to wait for the game to download and install then.

PlayStation 5 users, unfortunately, don't have it so simple. And there's no guarantee that this will work either. So, before we go any further, know that it just might not be worth the time and effort.

PlayStation accounts are region-locked, so Sony knows exactly where you're based when you're signed into your account.

If you want to attempt to access GTA 6 early on your PS5, create a new PSN account while using a VPN with a New Zealand-based location. From there, you'll actually have to purchase the game under this new account in the New Zealand PlayStation Store. As PCMag points out, this might even cost more due to currency conversions.

And, again, there is no guarantee that this will work.

Worst case, you have to wait another 18 hours before you can play a game you've already waited 13 years for.

#608. Germany's Gen Z protests disrupted by violence on Saturday

Nationwide protests led by young people were largely peaceful throughout the day, but reports about looting and rioting in the evening, especially in Frankfurt, overshadowed the spirit of the demonstrations.

This is a round-up of events at the youth protests across Germany on October 31 and November 1, 2026.

The Gen Z protests in Germany were mostly peaceful throughout the day, with tens of thousands of people having participated across big and smaller cities.

The peaceful demonstrations were overshadowed by reports about violence in some cities like Frankfurt (see below).

Hesse's state interior minister said he suspects that about 100 left-wing extremists instigated the violence in Frankurt.

There were instances of disturbances in Cologne, Hamburg and Bremen, too.

Riots, looting and attacks on police broke out in several German cities after protests by tens of thousands of young people across the country demanding better schools, relief from rising living costs and greater social justice.

The demonstrations had been largely peaceful during the day.

But serious disturbances erupted in the evening in several places.

Clashes broke out in Cologne on Saturday, with about 200 people involved in disturbances near Cologne Cathedral.

Police officers were attacked on the square outside the famous cathedral, with bottles and bicycles hurled toward them.

In a nearby side street, a window was smashed by an electric scooter thrown during the unrest, police said.

According to regional broadcaster WDR, other groups besides Gen Z demonstrators were involved in riots.

Cologne's police chief Johannes Hermanns said it was deeply saddening that peaceful protests were overshadowed by "extremists who had nothing but violence in mind."

While Gen Z protests across Germany were largely peaceful during the day, clashes were reported in several cities as night fell.

German police sealed off a major shopping street in central Frankfurt on Saturday night after rioters smashed shop windows, looted stores and attacked officers following a demonstration.

Police closed Die Zeil, one of Germany's busiest shopping streets, to incoming visitors and urged bystanders to leave the area.

"Anyone not involved who is still on the Zeil can leave. Access to the Zeil is no longer possible," Frankfurt police said in a post on X and in loudspeaker announcements.

Chaotic scenes unfolded along the shopping street, where dpa journalists witnessed people breaking into stores and stealing trainers and other goods.

A specialist firearms shop was also targeted, prompting several arrests, a police spokesman said.

Police also reported attacks on officers, including attacks involving incendiary devices.

The violence erupted after police broke up a demonstration organized as part of the nationwide "Gen Z regelt" (roughly meaning "Gen Z takes charge") protests.

A large contingent of officers was deployed around the Zeil, with authorities advising people to avoid the area or leave central Frankfurt.

The German protests on Saturday are a part of a wider trend that has seen members of Gen Z, born between 1997 and 2012, protest in several European nations.

The wave of protest was triggered by students seeking education reform in France, with the standoff erupting in violence and looting two weeks ago.

For our standalone story on protests in France today, click here.

After a day of youth protests in Germany, senior police union representative Andreas Rosskopf said that there was no widespread property damage "so far."

"The Gen Z protests have turned out to be very peaceful," Rosskopf told the daily Rhenische Post.

While confrontations were reported after the marches ended in multiple cities, the people driving the clashes were "individuals acting independently, some of whom were masked."

Rosskopf, who represents Germany's federal police, said security forces acted very decisively and forcefully when such response was appropriate.

"Security forces remain absolutely ready to prevent any further clashes in the late evening of overnight," he said.

German security forces reported minor violent incidents in several cites in the wake of the Gen Z demonstrations.

In Hamburg, protesters at the city's Steintor square pelted the police with fireworks . Police used "immediate force" to clear the area, including using a water cannon.

Several police officers were injured during a similar incident in Frankfurt, according to a state interior minister.

Police also used a water cannon in Cologne, where the march was halted and turned into a stationary rally after some protesters covered their faces and used pyrotechnics.

A police officers sustained light injuries in nearby Bonn during a confrontation with a group of protesters.

In Berlin, the authorities noted a rally separate from the official event organized by the Gen Z movement. Police initially reported "isolated instances of throwing eggs and bottles" from a crowd of around 500 people. The authorities later also reported "illegal burning of pyrotechnics" and said the crowd has grown to around 3,000 participants.

Several police officers were injured in a clash with a group of protesters following the Gen Z demonstration in Frankfurt, authorities said.

"One officers could be injured more seriously, but this will need some more looking into," said Hesse Interior Minister Roman Poseck.

"We assume there were about 100 attackers motivated by extreme leftist ideology," the state minister said.

"They have staged a massive attack against the police by throwing bottles, stones and fireworks."

Police responded with water cannons and have the situation in hand, he said

Thousands of young people took part in protests in 34 German cities on Saturday.

German Gen Z protesters called out rising living expenses, remilitarization of Germany, and declining education.

Some of the protesters also called for Germany's current chancellor, center-right Friedrich Merz, to step down.

The protests were held under the slogan Gen Z regelt (Gen Z sorts it).

Police were out in force after many politicians warned that Germany will not tolerate the kind of violence seen in France in mid-October.

Police reported incidents in which pepper spray and water cannon were used to keep crowds under control, with protesters setting off fireworks and lighting fires.

Most of the demonstrations ended peacefully.

But tensions remained high in some German cities with reports of several police officers injured.

In Germany's second-biggest city, Hamburg, police estimated 6,700 people taking part in the demonstration.

They reported some groups of black-clad protesters, some of whom also wore face masks, pulling apart construction site barriers and throwing them on the street. Some of the barriers were later set on fire.

Police said they pushed the crowd back and used pepper spray to break them apart. The fire was eventually put out.

Following an initial estimate of several hundred people attending the rally in central Berlin, police said that some 5,000 people were now gathered at the Brandenburg Gate. The organizers, "Gen Z regelt" (Gen Z sorts it) gave a much higher number, saying 10,000 people were in attendance.

One of the speakers in Berlin, Kaja Schwab, decried false promises made by politicians.

The youth is being told that "we will do well if we work hard enough." In reality, the life is getting unaffordable and the young are "forced into military service," she said, in reference to Germany's renewed recruitment drive.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Thousands of young people have joined the demonstrations in over 30 German cities, with police reporting largely peaceful protests.

Hundreds also gathered in Hamburg, Erfurt, Magdeburg, Dresden, Leipzig,  Nuremberg, and elsehwere.

Retailers in several city centers had boarded up shop windows, particularly along luxury shopping streets, fearing unrest. Some shops were already closed for the Reformation Day public holiday.

No nationwide turnout figure was immediately available. More than 182,100 people had expressed interest in attending the events online.

Police in Cologne called off the planned "Gen Z regelt" procession after some participants covered their faces and used pyrotechnics.

"The demonstration will continue as a stationary rally," a police spokeswoman told the DPA news agency. Participants would remain on the Rhine riverbank, she said, appealing for restraint.

Attendance remained below the 15,000 people registered for the demonstration. Based on advance registrations, Cologne's protest was expected to be the largest in North Rhine-Westphalia.

Police repeatedly stopped a youth protest march in Stuttgart, citing participants covering their faces and leaving the agreed route.

Officers also reported smoke devices and firecrackers before the procession began. "Be loud, but remain peaceful," a police spokeswoman urged in a video.

In other German cities, police reported a largely peaceful start to demonstrations. Authorities estimated included 2,500 participants in Freiburg, more than 1,500 in Frankfurt, 1,200 in Mainz, 1,000 in Munich and 650 in Berlin.

No nationwide turnout figure was immediately available.

Politicians must involve young people in decision-making or risk the youth turning away from political institutions, education researcher Nina Kolleck warned.

Their exclusion "creates the impression that there is a policy for the old, but not for the young," the University of Potsdam professor told Germany's RBB Inforadio.

Kolleck pointed to decades of underinvestment in schools and the disproportionate impact of climate change on younger generations.

She warned that populist parties could exploit the resulting political vacuum if young people's frustrations continued to go unanswered.

#607. MIT scientists break a 20-year rule and unlock never-before-seen crystal structures

Scientists have spent decades trying to control how tiny particles connect to form advanced materials. Now, researchers at MIT and their collaborators have discovered that doing the exact opposite of what was previously believed necessary can produce remarkable results.

Instead of relying on rigid molecular connections to hold nanoparticles in carefully planned arrangements, the team developed extremely flexible connectors that bend and adjust as particles come together. This unexpected strategy gives scientists a new way to control how nanoparticles organize themselves, allowing them to create crystal structures that have never been observed before.

The discovery could help overcome a major obstacle in materials science and open new possibilities for creating substances with precisely engineered properties. Potential applications include electronics, medicine, energy technologies, agriculture, and chemical manufacturing.

The findings, described in a paper that will appear in Nature Materials, demonstrate how the flexibility and electrical charges of molecular connectors can determine the structures that nanoparticles form.

MIT Researchers Challenge 20 Years of Materials Science

"People are interested in nanoparticle superlattices because of the promise of building designer materials where you have more say in what types of structures they can actually build into," says Rob Macfarlane, the Richard P. Simmons (1953) Professor in Metallurgy in MIT's Department of Materials Science and Engineering. "This is a new approach in nanoparticle assembly that hasn't been investigated before. It's exciting to have a new tool that is so counterintuitive. It's the exact opposite of what the dogma has been for 20 years: that you need to make connector ligands rigid, and any deviation causes assembly to fail. We showed if you just crank it all the way to the opposite extreme, it works just as well."

The research team also included MIT PhD candidate Nicholas Sbalbi, University of Delaware doctoral student Stephen Kronenberger, MIT undergraduate Hana Shinzawa, Matthew Ye PhD '26, and Arthi Jayaraman, a former professor at the University of Delaware.

At the heart of the discovery is a basic principle of materials science: The way a material's smallest components are arranged determines how that material behaves.

"That means if you know what your building blocks are and how they're arranged, you can explain what properties materials have," Macfarlane says. "Controlling that is how you make materials that have new properties."

This principle is especially important when working with nanoparticles, which are extremely small pieces of matter whose shapes, sizes, and properties can be adjusted for different purposes. Scientists already use individual nanoparticles in technologies involving drug delivery, energy storage, computing, and sensors.

But turning these tiny building blocks into larger, organized materials presents a difficult challenge.

Why Nanoparticles Are So Difficult to Control

One of the biggest obstacles is controlling how nanoparticles attach to one another. Scientists need to determine not only how many neighboring particles each nanoparticle connects with, but also the directions in which those connections form.

Without that control, nanoparticles tend to assemble into tightly packed arrangements that restrict the variety of structures researchers can produce. This limits their ability to create materials with unusual or specialized properties.

Researchers have traditionally approached the problem in two ways. One strategy involves changing the shapes of nanoparticles to influence how they fit together. Another involves modifying specific areas of their surfaces so that only certain regions attract neighboring particles.

In effect, scientists attempt to control where the particles stick to one another, much like designing puzzle pieces that can connect only in particular positions.

Although these methods can produce useful structures, they are often complicated, highly specialized, and difficult to adapt for large-scale production.

"The challenge with both of those approaches is they're difficult to do synthetically as we make the particles," Macfarlane explains. "The methods for defining stickiness that have been developed are always bespoke: They work for one material, at one size scale, in one condition. It's good for studying, but you can't do much with it."

Both strategies also depend on molecular connectors called ligands. These molecules attach to the surfaces of nanoparticles and help link neighboring particles together.

Traditionally, researchers have tried to make these ligands rigid so the connections remain at carefully controlled angles. This helps maintain a desired arrangement, but it also restricts the types of structures that can form and the functions they can perform.

The MIT team decided to explore a radically different possibility.

A Surprising Discovery About Flexible Molecular Bonds

Rather than forcing molecular connectors to remain in fixed positions, the researchers wondered whether giving them almost complete freedom to bend could offer an entirely new form of control.

"We thought, 'Let's do the exact opposite: make the bonds so flexible it doesn't matter what direction they're initially pointing.' The ligands can then reorganize as the particles come together, and that reorganization itself limits how many neighbors each particle can bind," Macfarlane says.

The idea reverses the usual approach to nanoparticle assembly. Instead of controlling the orientation of every connection in advance, the scientists allow the connectors to adjust naturally as the particles interact.

Macfarlane's laboratory has spent years developing ways to construct different types of nanoparticles using attached polymer chains. Polymers are large molecules made of repeating smaller units, and their flexibility makes them useful for creating adjustable molecular connections.

For the new system, the team equipped nanoparticles with highly flexible ligands that carry electrical charges at their ends. Some have positive charges, while others have negative charges.

Because opposite electrical charges attract, the connector molecules naturally bend toward partners with the opposite charge. This attraction helps the nanoparticles join together, while the flexibility of the connectors influences how many connections each particle can make.

"The idea is, instead of defining a specific direction the bonds are going to occur in with complicated synthesis methods, we just said, 'The bonds are going to be as flexible as they want to be, and they'll spontaneously go to whatever valency is going to maximize bond stability,'" Macfarlane says.

In this context, valency refers to the number of connections a nanoparticle forms with its neighbors. By allowing the connectors to move freely, the researchers found that the system could naturally settle into stable arrangements without requiring every connection to be designed beforehand.

Scientists Create Crystal Structures Never Seen Before

Experiments led by Sbalbi demonstrated that the researchers could adjust the connections between nanoparticles by changing two relatively straightforward characteristics: the sizes of the particles and the lengths of their flexible molecular chains.

These adjustments altered how the particles assembled, giving the team control over the number of neighboring particles each one could connect with.

Most importantly, the researchers used this method to produce previously unseen crystal structures.

Crystals are materials whose building blocks form organized, repeating patterns. In this case, the repeating arrangements are made from nanoparticles rather than individual atoms or small molecules. Such ordered nanoparticle networks are often called superlattices.

By reducing the number of connections between neighboring particles, the team was able to create more open arrangements instead of the densely packed structures that commonly form during nanoparticle assembly.

"Without having to predesign where the particles connect or what their shapes are, we can control the number of bonds each particle has," Macfarlane explains. "The amount of flexibility of the polymer dictates how many bonds it has. It allows us to lower the number of bonds each particle has and make lattices we have never seen before."

The results suggest that molecular flexibility, once viewed as an obstacle to precise nanoparticle assembly, can instead become a powerful tool for engineering new material structures.

A New Path Toward Customizable Designer Materials

The researchers believe their method could bring scientists closer to a long-sought goal in materials science: choosing the properties of individual nanoparticles independently of the larger structures into which they assemble.

Ideally, scientists could select nanoparticles for their electrical, optical, chemical, or other useful characteristics and then organize those particles into whatever arrangement best serves a particular application.

In practice, however, existing assembly methods have made that level of flexibility difficult to achieve.

"We in the nanoparticle assembly community talk about having completely independent control over what your particle is and what assembly it goes into," Macfarlane says. "In theory, that should be the case. In reality, it absolutely has not been."

The new approach could help close that gap. Because the researchers can influence nanoparticle arrangements through the flexibility of their connectors and the attraction between electrical charges, they may be able to create a wider variety of structures without the complicated manufacturing techniques required by traditional methods.

The team also sees the discovery as a promising route toward producing customizable materials at larger scales, potentially helping move nanoparticle technologies beyond laboratory experiments and into practical use.

Potential Applications in Electronics, Medicine, and Energy

The ability to build more open and varied nanoparticle structures could prove particularly valuable for developing advanced materials.

In photonics, which involves controlling and manipulating light, precisely organized nanoparticles could help researchers engineer materials with specialized optical properties. In chemical catalysis, where substances accelerate chemical reactions, new particle arrangements could create opportunities to improve the way catalysts operate.

The approach may also support future developments in medicine, agriculture, electronics, and energy technologies.

A major advantage is that nanoparticles can already possess a wide range of desirable properties. By controlling how those particles come together, scientists may be able to combine their individual capabilities in new ways.

"Nanoparticle superlattices offer a way to create designer materials where your building blocks have all sort sorts of unique properties," Macfarlane says. "But just densely packing these nanoparticles together limits your applications. This offers a way to get less dense formations of nanoparticles, and that's where a lot of the interesting applications are."

Although further development will be needed to translate the method into commercial technologies, the discovery establishes molecular flexibility as a new strategy for creating materials with tailored structures.

Instead of treating bending molecular connections as a problem to eliminate, scientists may now be able to use that flexibility to unlock arrangements that rigid designs could not easily achieve.

The research received partial support from the National Science Foundation, the Department of Energy, the U.S. Army, and the U.S. Navy.

SpaceX just launched a classified mission for the U.S. military.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base this evening (Nov. 6) at 7:48 p.m. EST (4:48 p.m. local California time; 0048 GMT on Nov. 7), rising into the sky as the sun sank toward the Pacific.

The launch kicked off the USSF-432 mission for the U.S. Space Force, which we know little about. Neither SpaceX nor the Space Force told us much about USSF-432 beforehand, and we learned tonight; SpaceX cut its webcast off about 10 minutes into the flight, shortly after the Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth for a landing.

That touchdown occurred aboard the SpaceX droneship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed downrange in the Pacific Ocean. It wrapped up the eighth flight for this particular booster, which is designated 1095.

The Falcon 9's upper stage, meanwhile, continued carrying its mystery payload skyward. It could be headed to low Earth orbit, outside observers speculate.

"It is possibly a batch of classified LEO satellites for the USSF's Space Based Sensing and Targeting (SBST) portfolio based on SpaceX's Starshield satellite bus, based on locations of rocket stage drop zones being exact fits with previous Starlink Group 15 launches," NextSpaceflight.com wrote in a mission description.

Starlink is SpaceX's LEO broadband megaconstellation, which consists of more than 11,000 active satellites. Starshield is a similar system designed to provide services to the U.S. military and its allies. Starshield satellites are believed to be based heavily on the Starlink spacecraft bus.

USSF-432 was the 119th Falcon 9 launch of 2026, and the 14th national-security flight of the rocket so far this year. The vast majority of Falcon 9 missions in 2026 — more than 70% — have been devoted to building out the Starlink megaconstellation.

SpaceX has also launched six other missions this year. Three were operational flights of the company's Falcon Heavy rocket, while the other three were test missions of its next-gen Starship vehicle. SpaceX plans to retire both the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy shortly after the fully reusable Starship, the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built, is up and running.

#605. Cheaper cars are selling considerably faster than at the beginning of the year

Consumers are concerned about rising fuel prices and affordability — and that could be showing up in how fast the least expensive cars are moving off dealer lots.

From the first quarter to the third, the number of days it took a dealer to sell a vehicle priced between $20,000 and $29,999 dropped 20%, according to data from Edmunds. That pace of selling saw the biggest acceleration of any price segment.

Vehicles priced from $30,000 to $39,999 sold about 18% faster, and the number of days it took to sell the next tier — $40,000 to $49,999 — dropped nearly 12%, according to Edmunds.

All of those price segments also took fewer days to turn than their more expensive counterparts. The lower-priced tiers took under 60 days to move off lots, with the least expensive ones selling the fastest. Every segment of vehicles above $50,000, meanwhile, took more than 60 days to sell.

"If you're a dealer and you have inventory and that price point, you're definitely noticing," said Edmunds Director of Insights Ivan Drury.

Cheaper vehicles may be selling faster, but they're still hard to find. The average listing price for a new vehicle in September was $49,726, according to Cox Automotive.

And, the overall sales numbers for some key segments priced under $40,000 have fallen. This has especially been true for compact cars, which are down roughly 4% since the beginning of 2026, and compact SUVs, down nearly 8% in the same period, according to Cox Automotive.

These different data points seem to be moving in opposite directions. On the one hand, cheaper cars are moving faster off dealer lots. On the other, sales of affordable segments are down.

There are a few reasons for this, according to analysts who follow the industry. One is that there might not be enough lower-priced vehicles on dealer lots in the first place.

"I think there are some supply things going on at that end of the market," said Cox Automotive Deputy Chief Economist Mark Strand. "We have to kind of grade the market on a curve until we see what's going on with fourth-quarter data."

The compact SUV segment, in particular, is suffering from the lack of two popular models.

The Toyota RAV4, which is the most popular SUV in the U.S., has been in short supply at many dealerships this year, as the automaker shifts production to its Kentucky factory, Strand said. The company also has shifted the entire lineup to a hybrid powertrain at a time when hybrids have been in exceptionally high demand.

The other missing SUV is the Ford Escape, which that automaker discontinued to make way for its upcoming midsize EV pickup truck.

The other slow-selling, low-priced segment — compact cars — faces structural inventory challenges, said AutoForecast Solutions Vice President of Global Forecasting Sam Fiorani.

"We've seen the disappearance of affordable, compact new vehicles over the last decade," he said.

Detroit automakers swapped out their lineups of compact coupes and sedans in favor of small crossover SUVs, which tend to carry slightly higher sticker prices than comparably sized passenger cars.

Currently, there is not a single compact passenger sedan for sale by an American manufacturer. Most on the market are Japanese or Korean, with a few German models, such as the Volkswagen Jetta and the Golf hatchback.

"You have all these brands that have just abandoned the marketplace," Fiorani said.

The smallest American passenger cars are the Ford Mustang, General Motors' Chevrolet Corvette, and the midsize Tesla Model 3 sedan, according to AutoForecast Solutions. The firm classifies both the Mustang and the Corvette as sports cars, and as such they occupy a different niche than compact sedans like the Honda Civic or Toyota Corolla.

The Mustang has a starting price of $33,490, the Model 3 starts at $34,990 and the Chevrolet Corvette starts at $71,300. Cars like the Civic, Corolla and Jetta, meanwhile, all start below $25,000.

"Compact vehicle buyers are very price-sensitive," Fiorani said. "And so when the price of gas goes up, that eats into their car payment. That means that they can't afford a $500 or $600 a month car payment, and they have to move into the used market."

Indeed, the wholesale used prices of compact cars have risen and are up more than almost any other segment, according to Cox Automotive. Wholesale prices — the prices vehicles sell for at large auctions, like Cox Automotive's Manheim auction — are indicators for prices overall in the fragmented used-car market.

Along with the rise in prices, auto finance stats show that a historically high number of buyers are stretching to afford cars.

Roughly one in four buyers financing their purchases are getting 84-month loans — a record. Nearly 3 in 10 trade-ins toward new-vehicle purchases carried negative equity in the third quarter, meaning the cars being traded in were worth less than the outstanding balances of the loans on them. Shoppers are often rolling these negative balances into new loans, which pushes up the new payment cost.

Automakers have also been more tightly aligning production with demand to avoid discounting vehicles. Incentives on average are about 6.6% of the average transaction price as of October, according to Cox Automotive. Leasing offers a way to get a car with a lower payment, but leasing rates are also down.

Vehicle trade-in data suggests that many buyers who are snapping up those fast-selling cheaper vehicles are either first-time buyers or are purchasing supplemental vehicles, Edmunds' Drury said.

The subcompact SUV segment is one lower-priced group that has seen sales rise in 2026. That is a segment that attracts a lot of first-time buyers. But this is still a relatively small share of the total car market, Fiorani said.

"It's not the mainstream vehicle that Americans want," he said. "It is the vehicle that entry-level buyers need to get to work, to get to school. ... It's people who don't have families yet."

Repeat buyers are less likely to want to step down into a compact car or SUV, Drury said.

"The moment you get into that other vehicle and it's a little bit smaller, it's not as comfortable, it doesn't fit all your stuff, all your kid's equipment for soccer practice, you're done," he said. "You're not giving up 360 cameras, ventilated seats, heated steering wheels, these niceties that you've become accustomed to. Automakers know that too. Dealers know that."

The truly cash-strapped are either snapping up the relatively few low-priced cars on dealer lots, moving to the used market, or holding on to their cars longer.

"The people who are trying to buy the smaller vehicles are really hurt by the way the economy is at the moment," Fiorani said. "So those people are trying to move into used vehicles or trying to maintain their current vehicle as long as they can. Automakers should be prepared for a softening in the marketplace."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman is serious about launching "big rockets" to the moon every single year for the agency's Artemis program. And the new space race with China is fueling that ambition.

"I feel good. I feel like we are certainly on a more achievable path to the lunar surface today than where we were before," Isaacman told Space.com.

We recently sat down with the NASA chief to discuss the state of the Artemis program, and, off the bat, he made it clear that he's confident in the U.S. space program following the success of April's Artemis II mission around the moon. In fact, just prior to our conversation, it was announced that Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman will become the new deputy director of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. But the road from Artemis II's success to crewed lunar landings and, later, a permanent moon base will take a lot of launches of NASA's Space Launch System (SLS) megarocket, Isaacman stressed.

"You know, a lot of people, especially in the space community, start getting [into] if the landers are there or not. I don't really care about that right now. What I care about is that we are launching big rockets no less than once a year," he said.

"I think that's imperative for NASA to be doing these deep-space human spaceflight missions right now," Isaacman added. "So, we had a great mission in April of '26. We will launch again in '27."

That coming launch will be for Artemis III, a crewed mission to low Earth orbit that will test docking procedures between NASA's Orion capsule and one or both of the Artemis program's private lunar landers — SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon.

"We need to continue to exercise those muscles," he said, referring to SLS liftoffs. "And, honestly, once a year isn't great, either. I mean, I don't think we're going to get back to the early [space] shuttle days, you know, four missions a year. I don't think we're going to get back to where we were with Apollo, but once a year is the minimum … I would testify that to Congress in this role years down the road.

"If NASA is going to be doing deep-space missions, complicated missions, [we should] launch at least once a year and get as much out of it as you can for taking the risk and spending the taxpayer dollars and building towards something greater," Isaacman added. "That's what we're doing with Artemis III, and that's what's going to better prepare us for Artemis IV."

So, how is NASA coping with the challenges that face them as they approach Artemis III ahead of a crewed lunar landing on Artemis IV, which is targeted for 2028? While NASA can learn some lessons from past moon missions with Apollo, today it's primarily relying on the extensive experience and talent within the agency, according to Isaacman.

"Artemis II is very different from Apollo 8, and Artemis III will be very different from Apollo 9," he said. "Our approach is not exactly the same as it was … But what is the same right now? The spirit, the energy, the potential within NASA. The talent of the workforce and industry is no different than the 1960s."

There's another similarity to the Apollo era: NASA has a rival in its race to the moon. While the adversary in the 1960s was the Soviet Union, today the U.S. is competing against China.

"It is a real space race," Isaacman said. But, he added, "this one is very different than the first one."

"Everything is closer than it was, not just in space. I mean, we had the edge in computing [and] every one of the technology domains during the Cold War. Our capabilities were better by a mile," he said. "[But with] China, it's not [like that]. They're very close."

"We're saying we're going to land on the moon at the end of 2028. China is saying by the end of 2029," Isaacman added. "And it's like, Well, are they going to pull it off? Yes, they will. They've showcased their landers, their rovers, their suits, two-launch architecture with built-in reusability."

So NASA is taking the Chinese threat very seriously, according to Isaacman.

"The consequence of getting this wrong, I'm telling you — it's going to be felt around the world," he said. "It will call everything into question."

"Should I be using American superintelligence or AI? Should I be doing Chinese? Should I be buying their computers? Should I be [buying] ours? Buying their cars, their airplanes, their ships? Whose security guarantees to trust?" Isaacman added. "I think the implications are pretty severe, which is why we're taking it so seriously and putting such extreme focus on the mission right now. But we have that playbook of success, and I think we will prevail."

#602. A dead star's mysterious rings reveal what could happen when our Sun dies

Astronomers have discovered an extraordinary ring of planetary wreckage around a dead star, offering a possible preview of what could happen to our own Solar System billions of years from now. Even more surprising, the debris is divided into two distinct rings, with a clear gap between them that may be maintained by planetary bodies that somehow survived their star's death.

The discovery was made using the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope (ESO's VLT). Unlike previously observed debris systems around dead stars, this one appears to contain two separate discs of material left behind by destroyed planets. Researchers believe two surviving objects may be shaping the unusual structure, including one potentially as large as Pluto or even the Moon.

"We have known for some time that planets may survive beyond the transformation of their central star, but this is the first example of a complex system with a double debris disc and potentially two surviving planetesimals," says Nicola Gentile Fusillo, an astronomer at the Università degli Studi di Trieste in Italy and lead author of the study published in Nature Astronomy.

A Dead Star Surrounded by Planetary Wreckage

At the center of the system is J1328−1450, a white dwarf. These extremely dense stellar remnants form when stars similar to our Sun exhaust their fuel and reach the final stages of their evolution. After expanding dramatically and shedding their outer layers, they leave behind their exposed cores.

This transformation can be catastrophic for nearby planets. As a star swells, it may engulf and destroy worlds orbiting too close to it. More distant rocky objects can survive the initial upheaval, although gravitational disturbances may eventually tear some of them apart. Their remains can form rotating discs of debris around the dead star.

Astronomers have observed such debris discs around other white dwarfs, but J1328−1450 is different. Instead of a single ring of vaporized planetary material, it has two concentric rings, meaning one lies farther from the star than the other. The rings remain clearly separated, creating an unusual structure that scientists are now trying to explain.

"The structure we see in this system is particularly intriguing because the two gaseous rings are remarkably stable and remain separated by a gap," says co-author Felipe Lagos-Vilches, an astronomer at the University of Warwick, UK, and at the Universidad Técnica Federico Santa María in Chile.

"The system is a rare glimpse of the violent, chaotic process by which a planetary system meets its end, and it hints that dead stars can have disc structures far more complex than previously realized," adds Gentile Fusillo, who is also affiliated with the INAF-Astronomical Observatory of Trieste.

Two Surviving Worlds May Be Shaping the Rings

The researchers suspect that two surviving planetary bodies, each traveling along a separate orbit, are responsible for maintaining the double ring structure.

One of these objects, associated with the inner ring, is thought to be comparable in size to a typical asteroid, measuring only a few kilometers across. The other, farther from the star, could be much larger, potentially reaching the size of Pluto or even our Moon.

Such objects are known as planetesimals, a term used for smaller solid bodies associated with the formation and evolution of planetary systems. Although the two suspected survivors have not been directly observed, their gravitational influence could help explain why the debris remains organized into two distinct rings rather than forming one continuous disc.

The evidence comes from observations collected with the X-Shooter instrument on ESO's VLT in Chile's Atacama Desert. The instrument analyzes light across a broad range of wavelengths, allowing astronomers to examine the chemical makeup and motion of material surrounding distant objects.

Previously discovered debris discs around white dwarfs have shared a recognizable observational signature consistent with a single, flat, rotating disc. J1328−1450 breaks that pattern. Its observations instead reveal the unique fingerprint of a double disc, providing evidence of a far more complicated arrangement of planetary remains.

Chemical Clues Reveal the Remains of Destroyed Planets

The debris also contains important clues about the worlds that once orbited the star.

Astronomers detected calcium, oxygen, magnesium, and iron, elements commonly found in rocky planetary material throughout our Solar System. Their presence indicates that the rings contain remnants of solid bodies rather than simply gas left over from the star itself.

More intriguingly, the two rings have noticeably different chemical compositions. The inner ring contains substantial amounts of magnesium gas, while the outer ring is largely depleted of magnesium.

This difference suggests that the material in the two rings may have originated from separate planets with different compositions. If so, the system could preserve evidence of multiple destroyed worlds.

Another possibility is that both rings contain material from different layers of the same planetary body. For example, one ring could contain debris from a planet's outer crust, while the other contains material from deeper inside, such as its core.

Either explanation would offer valuable insight into the destruction of rocky worlds and the complex processes that can continue long after a star has exhausted its fuel.

A Possible Preview of Our Solar System's Future

The discovery also raises a compelling question about the ultimate fate of our own planetary neighborhood.

Billions of years from now, the Sun will undergo a similar transformation. It will expand into a red giant, shed its outer layers, and eventually become a white dwarf. During this process, the inner Solar System will experience enormous changes, and Earth itself may be destroyed.

Yet the observations of J1328−1450 suggest that the death of a star does not necessarily mean the complete disappearance of its planetary system. Some objects may survive, while others could be shattered into debris that continues orbiting the stellar remnant in complex arrangements.

By studying this distant dead star and its unusual double rings, astronomers are gaining a rare opportunity to investigate what remains after a planetary system experiences such a violent transformation.

"The system therefore offers a remarkable glimpse of what the future of planetary systems, including systems like our own, might look like," concludes Lagos-Vilches.

Materials provided by European Southern Observatory. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
